articles.title: How the Philippines fell behind its Asean peers - Inquirer.net
articles.summary: How the Philippines fell behind its Asean peers  Inquirer.net
articles.full_text:
In the decades immediately following World War II, the Philippines was widely regarded as one of Asia’s most promising economies. During the 1950s and early 1960s, it enjoyed relatively high income levels, strong educational attainment and an industrial base that compared favorably with many of its Southeast Asian neighbors.
Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and even war-ravaged Vietnam looked to various aspects of Philippine governance, education and institutional development as reference points.
Yet by the early 21st century, the Philippines had fallen behind most of its Asean peers in industrialization, productivity growth, export sophistication, rural transformation and poverty reduction.
The country’s relative decline cannot be explained by a single factor. Rather, it reflects the interaction of five long-term structural forces: colonial and postcolonial economic dependence institutionalized through the Bell Trade Act and related economic arrangements; the persistence of a stabilization-oriented development paradigm associated with the Dodge Report and subsequent IMF-World Bank conditionalities; chronic indebtedness reinforced by automatic debt-servicing mechanisms under Presidential Decree No. 1177; systemic corruption that diverted public resources away from productive investment and social development; and the failure to sustain industrialization and technological upgrading.
Rapid population growth, environmental degradation, agricultural stagnation, energy dependence and governance weaknesses further magnified these structural constraints.
The result is an economy characterized by low industrial capacity, extensive labor export, high infrastructure costs, persistent food insecurity and recurring fiscal stress despite decades of respectable gross domestic product growth.
Drawing lessons from the experiences of South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, China and Vietnam, this paper concludes that the Philippines requires a comprehensive national transformation strategy centered on industrial policy, technological upgrading, anti-corruption reforms, agricultural modernization, population stabilization and debt restructuring.
Without such reforms, the country risks remaining trapped in a cycle of dependence, inequality and underdevelopment despite its substantial human and natural resources.
Few development puzzles in Asia are as striking as the Philippine experience.
At the dawn of independence in 1946, the Philippines possessed many advantages. It had one of the highest literacy rates in Asia, significant natural resources, democratic institutions, English-language proficiency and a relatively developed urban economy. During the 1950s and early 1960s, it was among the region’s leading economies.
Yet by 2026, the country had been overtaken by Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and, increasingly, Vietnam.
Vietnam, despite experiencing decades of war and destruction, developed a strong manufacturing base and rapidly expanding export sector. Thailand became a major automotive manufacturing hub. Malaysia developed sophisticated electronics industries. Singapore transformed itself into a global financial and technological center.
The Philippines, in contrast, became increasingly dependent on remittances, overseas labor, imported manufactured goods, imported fuel, imported food and external financing.
Why Vietnam moved ahead of the Philippines
Vietnam provides perhaps the most revealing comparison.
Following decades of war, Vietnam faced conditions arguably worse than those confronting the Philippines. Yet it pursued land reform, industrial policy, export-oriented manufacturing, human capital investment and state-guided development.
The country aggressively attracted foreign direct investment while simultaneously building domestic productive capacity.
Today, Vietnam exports electronics, machinery, industrial goods and processed agricultural products. Its manufacturing sector plays a central role in economic growth.
The Philippines remains more dependent on services, remittances and imports.
Vietnam’s experience demonstrates that war alone does not determine developmental outcomes. Policy choices, institutions and industrial strategy matter.
Historical origins: Bell Trade Act and the foundations of dependency
The historical roots of the Philippines’ developmental stagnation lie primarily in missed industrialization opportunities compounded by debt dependence and systemic corruption.
The roots of Philippine underdevelopment can be traced to the economic arrangements established immediately after independence.
The Bell Trade Act of 1946 tied the Philippine economy closely to the United States through preferential trade arrangements, exchange-rate controls and parity rights that granted American citizens access comparable to that of Filipinos in exploiting natural resources, according to an account of the law by Encyclopaedia Britannica.
Critics argued that these provisions limited economic sovereignty and reinforced export dependence rather than domestic industrial development.
While the legislation provided access to reconstruction aid following World War II, it also encouraged continued specialization in primary commodities rather than the development of higher-value manufacturing sectors.
Instead of pursuing a developmental-state strategy similar to those later adopted by South Korea and Taiwan, the Philippines remained embedded in a dependent economic structure in which exports of agricultural commodities and imports of manufactured goods became the norm.
Economic historians have argued that this model delayed the emergence of a strong indigenous industrial bourgeoisie capable of driving technological modernization.
The Dodge Plan and the emphasis on fiscal conservatism
A second historical turning point emerged through American-sponsored stabilization programs commonly associated with the Dodge Report.
As discussed in a June 2026 Philippine Daily Inquirer commentary on the continuing influence of the Dodge framework on industrial policy, the approach emphasized macroeconomic stabilization, fiscal discipline, balanced budgets and debt repayment over aggressive industrial expansion.
While fiscal stability is important, the Philippine experience suggests that excessive emphasis on austerity constrained public investment in manufacturing, research and development, strategic infrastructure, industrial finance and technology development.
Countries that later became industrial powerhouses frequently tolerated temporary fiscal deficits while directing substantial investments toward industrial upgrading.
South Korea, Taiwan, China and Vietnam all relied on active state intervention, industrial planning, strategic protection and targeted subsidies.
The Philippines instead increasingly embraced a development model prioritizing debt service, financial stability and market liberalization.
The consequence was chronic underinvestment in industrial transformation.
The lost opportunity of the martial law era
The 1970s could have been a decisive decade for Philippine industrialization.
Many developing countries used similar periods to build industrial capacity, establish technological institutions and develop export competitiveness. Malaysia expanded manufacturing. Singapore accelerated technological upgrading. South Korea built globally competitive industrial conglomerates. Taiwan strengthened strategic industries.
Instead, the Philippine experience during martial law became increasingly associated with concentrated economic power, rent-seeking, crony capitalism, debt-financed infrastructure and growing external indebtedness.
While infrastructure projects expanded, institutional weaknesses prevented the emergence of broad-based industrial development.
The development strategy increasingly relied on foreign borrowing rather than productivity growth. Consequently, the economy accumulated debt faster than it accumulated productive capacity.
PD 1177 and the institutionalization of debt priority
A critical but often overlooked factor is Presidential Decree No. 1177.
The Budget Reform Decree of 1977 institutionalized automatic appropriations for debt servicing, effectively giving debt payments priority in public expenditures, according to the decree as published by the LawPhil Project.
Critics have argued that this framework created a structural bias in national budgeting.
Debt servicing remained protected even during periods when social services, education, agriculture and health care required expanded investment.
Department of Budget and Management documents on national government debt-service expenditures show debt-service obligations reaching trillions of pesos annually. Government debt-service expenditures exceeded P2 trillion in recent fiscal years.
The Bureau of the Treasury’s 2025 annual debt report likewise documents the scale of the government’s debt obligations.
The consequence is what may be termed a “crowding-out effect,” in which fiscal resources that could otherwise support agricultural modernization, irrigation systems, research institutions, science education, health care and climate-resilience programs are redirected toward servicing past obligations.
While debt repayment is necessary to maintain creditworthiness, excessive debt burdens can reduce developmental flexibility.
Debt dependence as a development trap
Development economists have long observed that debt can either stimulate or hinder growth.
Borrowing becomes productive when funds create assets that generate future economic returns. It becomes problematic when funds are lost through corruption, projects are poorly designed, returns cannot cover financing costs or borrowing finances consumption rather than production.
The Philippines increasingly faces risks associated with the latter scenario.

articles.title: Sembcorp wins conditional approval to import 1.3 GW of renewable power from Vietnam, Malaysia - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Sembcorp wins conditional approval to import 1.3 GW of renewable power from Vietnam, Malaysia  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Singapore’s Energy Market Authority (EMA) has granted conditional approval to Sembcorp Utilities, a wholly owned subsidiary of Sembcorp Industries, to import up to 1.3 gigawatts (GW) of renewable electricity from Vietnam and Malaysia through a regional power corridor.
The conditional approval was formally presented at the opening of Singapore International Energy Week 2026 on Monday.
Under the proposed arrangement, electricity generated by offshore wind farms in Vietnam would be transmitted through Malaysia to supply both the Malaysian and Singaporean markets.
Malaysia would serve as both a recipient and a transit country for the regional power flow. Imports are expected to begin in 2035, subject to further regulatory and project approvals.
The conditional approval provides a basis for the participating consortia to advance the next stages of project development, Sembcorp said in an announcement on Monday.
The Vietnam-Malaysia-Singapore (VMS) initiative aims to supply Singapore with low-carbon electricity by linking Vietnam’s offshore wind resources with solar power and battery energy storage infrastructure in Malaysia.
The initiative builds on a joint development agreement signed in May 2025 by two consortia. One comprises PetroVietnam Technical Services Corporation (PTSC), a member of Vietnam National Industry–Energy Group (Petrovietnam), and Sembcorp Utilities. The other, MY Energy Consortium, comprises Malaysia’s Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) and Petroliam Nasional Berhad (Petronas).
Since signing the agreement, the partners have advanced technical and commercial work in coordination with governments, regulators and other stakeholders across the three countries.

articles.title: How purchases of sanctioned Iranian jet fuel were disguised by Myanmar - The Straits Times
articles.summary: How purchases of sanctioned Iranian jet fuel were disguised by Myanmar  The Straits TimesRegime Disguises Military Jet Fuel as Diesel to Evade Sanctions: JFM  The IrrawaddyEXCLUSIVE: How purchases of sanctioned Iranian jet fuel were disguised by Myanmar  ReutersHow a Myanmar fuel deal obscured an Iranian jet-fuel shipment  Mezha.netMyanmar Jet Fuel Trade Fraud: $109.5M in Suspect Imports  Fincrime Central
articles.full_text:
AI generated
In December 2025, the US-sanctioned tanker Reef arrived in Myanmar waters with around 113,000 barrels of fuel backed by sham paperwork.
Myanmar-based energy broker Dynamic Wave ordered the shipment, agreeing in a sales contract inked with Thailand’s Tawan-Oil Trading to supposedly take delivery of a similar amount of South African diesel.
But the US$15.8 million (S$20.2 million) agreement, which Reuters viewed, was a charade: There was no such trade between South Africa and Myanmar in 2025, according to data from the United Nations and Vortexa, a shipping and energy data provider.
In reality, Reef carried jet fuel from Iran to Myanmar, according to records of fuel shipments to Myanmar, as well as satellite images and analysis by SynMax Intelligence, which tracked the tanker’s journey from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas to South-east Asia.
The deception was needed because the US in 2023 imposed targeted sanctions on Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry.
The US did so citing the deadly bombing campaign waged by the South-east Asian country’s military on civilian targets as part of an effort to crush a rebel-led insurgency. All purchasers of Iranian oil and fuel are also exposed to sweeping American sanctions.
Details of how Myanmar disguised purchases of Iranian jet fuel, as well as the entities involved in the transactions, are reported here for the first time.
Myanmar’s military junta was involved in the ruse. Days before Reef arrived, Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator told the client of Dynamic Wave that it would issue import documentation that labelled the delivery as diesel “instead of jet fuel”, according to a copy of the agency’s Nov 30 letter seen by Reuters. The document, which was provided to Reuters by the activist group Justice For Myanmar, did not explain the purpose of the mislabelling.
The letter from the regulator also authorised Dynamic Wave and its client, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Company, to pay Tawan for the shipment.
Neither Dynamic Wave nor its client, which is part-owned by Myanmar’s military-backed government, responded to questions about the fuel shipment.
Spokespeople for Myanmar’s military-backed government and foreign exchange regulator, and the Iranian Foreign Ministry also did not return requests for comment.
Tehran was the Myanmar military’s primary supplier of jet fuel between October 2024 and December 2025, with much of the trade carried out by the tankers Reef – since renamed Maris – and Noble, a Reuters report revealed in January.
The scheme uncovered by Reuters underscores both the reach and limits of Washington’s power.
The lengths taken to disguise the trade suggest US sanctions are biting. But Iranian jet fuel has continued to flow, earning Tehran valuable foreign currency and providing Myanmar with the means to conduct both commercial aviation and air raids.
The US Treasury did not respond to questions about jet-fuel shipments between Iran and Myanmar.
Jet fuel, air strikes and civilian casualties
Myanmar’s generals seized power in 2021 from the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi. The coup sparked a civil war, during which the military killed thousands – including many civilians – in aerial assaults, the UN said in August.
Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said in response to the UN allegations that the military “exercises maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm”.
Justice For Myanmar, which also shared the fuel sales contract with Reuters, published a report on Oct 26 concluding that Myanmar’s junta was importing jet fuel mislabelled as diesel.
The organisation, which supports further sanctions on Myanmar’s jet fuel imports, said it obtained the documents from a junta-run server that was briefly publicly accessible.
Reuters found a dead link to one of the documents on the DuckDuckGo search engine, indicating it had once been hosted on that server. Delivery dates and fuel quantities in the documents also match Iranian jet fuel shipment records that were separately reviewed by the news agency.
Thai bank connection
The sales contract for Dynamic Wave’s fuel shipment stipulated that the payment be transferred into Tawan’s account at Siam Commercial Bank (SCB), Thailand’s oldest bank.
Tawan was identified by UN experts in a 2024 report as a jet-fuel supplier to Myanmar’s military. The firm has not commented on those allegations.
SCB was described as a major facilitator of Myanmar military procurement in that report.
The bank said after the report’s release that it adheres to anti-money-laundering laws and that its Myanmar-related transactions were legitimate and not connected to the arms trade.
Reuters could not determine whether SCB was aware of the nature of Tawan’s business.
Thai regulators in 2024 ordered banks to closely scrutinise transactions involving Myanmar to comply with sanctions and anti-money-laundering laws.
SCB did not respond to repeated requests for comment about its commercial relationship with Tawan.
Tawan and the Bank of Thailand, which supervises the kingdom’s financial industry, also did not respond to questions.
The December shipment was not the first time jet fuel arrived in Myanmar disguised as diesel.
Dynamic Wave in May 2025 agreed to buy from Tawan 202,000 barrels of what a second contract, also obtained from the junta server, described as South African diesel.
The agreement stipulated that the diesel should arrive at Yangon within a month and that Dynamic Wave would pay US$26 million into Tawan’s SCB account.
The invoice for that contract contained discrepancies suggesting the tanker actually contained jet fuel.
The density of the fuel listed in the document matched the specifications for jet fuel rather than diesel sold in South-east Asia, according to Joshua Heyne, a jet-fuel expert at Washington State University, and data from Platts, the energy-industry information provider. The price of the fuel was also more than 50% higher than a global diesel benchmark.
Noble called at Yangon on June 17 carrying just under 200,000 barrels of jet fuel earmarked for Dynamic Wave, shipment records show.
Like Reef’s December shipment, Noble’s cargo was loaded at Iran’s Bandar Abbas, according to SynMax’s analysis of satellite imagery.
As it made its way to Myanmar’s commercial capital, Noble transmitted location signals that made it appear as though its destination was the port of Chittagong in Bangladesh, according to SynMax.
The manager of the Reef and Noble tankers did not respond to questions sent via its listed website.
Shipments of jet fuel between Iran and Myanmar have continued in 2026, Reuters reported in October, citing SynMax analysis and satellite imagery. REUTERS

articles.title: Linking FDI and domestic enterprises: A driving force for supporting industries. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Linking FDI and domestic enterprises: A driving force for supporting industries.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
From attracting investment to increasing domestic value creation.
 In the first eight months of 2026, the processing and manufacturing industry continued to lead in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), with over US$21 billion, accounting for 51.8% of the total registered investment capital. The presence of large corporations such as Samsung , LG, Toyota, Intel, and Hana Micron has contributed to making Vietnam an important link in the global production network and supply chain, while also creating a large market for supporting industrial enterprises.
 However, the expansion of production and exports does not necessarily translate into a corresponding increase in domestic added value. According to data shared by the Ministry of Industry and Trade at the Workshop on Supporting Industry Development on September 30, 2026, in 2025, the import value of goods and services increased by 17.12%, higher than the 16.27% increase in exports. Coupled with the dependence on imported raw materials, components, and spare parts in many key industries, this necessitates improving domestic supply capacity to better utilize the expansion of production activities. 
 Production line for camera modules and electronic components for export at the factory of MCNEX VINA Co., Ltd. in Phuc Son Industrial Park, Ninh Binh province.
 The challenge is not just to continue attracting more FDI projects, but more importantly, to transform the presence of multinational corporations into opportunities for developing Vietnam's technological capabilities, productivity, and business systems. This also represents a shift from a mindset focused on attracting FDI to one that enhances FDI absorption capacity, linking investment efficiency with the level of spillover effects on the domestic economy .
 In its presentation at the conference, the Ministry of Finance noted that the trend of shifting production according to the "China + 1" strategy opens up significant opportunities for countries receiving investment. However, the spillover effects can only be realized when local businesses have sufficient capacity to supply raw materials, components, and support services to meet the requirements of international production chains.
 In reality, the gap between domestic supporting industries and multinational corporations remains significant. According to statistics, out of approximately 1,000 enterprises capable of directly supplying assembly companies and multinational corporations, domestic enterprises account for only about 30%. Meanwhile, about 88% of supporting industry enterprises are small and medium-sized, largely limited in terms of capital, technology, management capacity, and access to market information.
 In particular, becoming a supplier for large corporations does not simply depend on the ability to produce a single type of component. Businesses must also simultaneously meet stringent requirements regarding quality, stability, delivery schedules, traceability, and continuous improvement capabilities. For high-tech components, the process of evaluating and selecting suppliers demands even more time, resources, and technical expertise.
 Therefore, focusing solely on financial incentives or isolated trade networking activities will not fundamentally address the capacity gaps. What Vietnamese businesses need is not only access to customers, but also the conditions to gradually meet standards, participate in production, and upgrade their position in the value chain.
 Developing domestic suppliers - key to improving FDI efficiency.
 The need to strengthen linkages between the FDI sector and domestic enterprises has been clearly defined in Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy. The resolution emphasizes enhancing the spillover effects of the FDI sector through technology transfer, human resource training, and the development of domestic suppliers. It also sets out the task of developing a national program for domestic supplier development, establishing a database, and creating a platform for connecting FDI enterprises with Vietnamese businesses.
 Furthermore, Government Decree No. 96/2026/ND-CP dated March 31, 2026, continues to identify the production of products on the list of priority supporting industrial products as a sector with special investment incentives. Prime Minister's Decision No. 929/QD-TTg dated May 25, 2026, approving the Program for the Development of Supporting Industries for the period 2026-2035, also emphasizes improving technological capacity, quality management, human resource training, and strengthening connections between domestic enterprises and leading enterprises.
 To both promote linkages between FDI and domestic enterprises and ensure compliance with international commitments, the policy for developing supporting industries needs to be continuously implemented and refined in a way that encourages cooperation based on the harmonious interests of all parties. This includes focusing on creating incentives for FDI enterprises to proactively develop their supplier networks in Vietnam, strengthening technology transfer, human resource training, and production linkages. Simultaneously, it focuses on enhancing the competitiveness of domestic enterprises, helping them gradually meet the requirements of global supply chains through product quality, productivity, and technological capabilities. 
 The Department of Industry will work with Samsung Vietnam in October 2026 to integrate Vietnamese businesses into the supply chain.
 Therefore, the appropriate approach is to create incentives for FDI enterprises to proactively develop suppliers in Vietnam through incentive mechanisms linked to technology transfer results, human resource training, product development, and enhanced linkages. At the same time, resources should be focused on supporting domestic enterprises to improve their capacity to compete and participate in supply chains based on product quality, productivity, and market responsiveness.
 From an industrial development perspective, three priority areas should be focused on: identifying product groups, components, and processes with the potential for localization, linked to the specific needs of large corporations; improving the database and supply-demand connection platform so that domestic businesses can access information, standards, and opportunities to participate in the supply chain; and implementing programs to upgrade suppliers in terms of management, technology, quality, and human resources according to the requirements of leading businesses in the supply chain.
 More importantly, support activities should aim for measurable results, such as the number of businesses becoming new suppliers, the percentage of products meeting international standards, the value of orders fulfilled, and the level of technological capacity increase of Vietnamese businesses.
 In the context of FDI continuing to play a crucial role in industrial development, enhancing the capacity to absorb and disseminate technology will determine the extent to which domestic enterprises can capitalize on opportunities. When large investment projects not only generate output and export revenue but also foster the formation of a capable supplier network, the nation's position will shift from an important production and assembly location to a higher-value link in the global industrial chain.

articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE: Singapore’s Energy Market Authority (EMA) and Malaysia’s Energy Commission (ST) today renewed their partnership to further strengthen bilateral cooperation in the energy sector during the 19th Singapore International Energy Week (SIEW).
In a joint statement, the regulators said the renewed memorandum of understanding (MoU) provides a framework for both regulators to strengthen technical cooperation, regulatory exchanges and knowledge sharing.
"The areas of cooperation include the planning and reliability of electricity and piped gas systems, regulation of wholesale and retail electricity markets, implementation of cross-border electricity trading projects, Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs), and interconnection capacity.
"The MoU will also strengthen collaboration on solar and energy storage systems,” they said.
The exchange of the MoU between EMA and ST was witnessed by Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof, who is also Energy Transition and Water Transformation Minister, and Singapore Energy, Trade and Industry Minister (Energy and Industry) Dr Tan See Leng at the opening of SIEW 2026 on Monday.
Meanwhile, EMA has granted conditional approval to Sembcorp Utilities Pte Ltd to import 1.3 gigawatts (GW) of electricity to Singapore with its consortium partners, MY Energy Consortium (MYEC), comprising Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas), Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB), and PetroVietnam Technical Services Corporation (PTSC).
The approval came following a joint development agreement signed on the sidelines of the 46th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, in May 2025.
The approval will allow Singapore to source and integrate low-carbon electricity from regional and domestic resources, including offshore wind from Vietnam and solar power from Malaysia.
"Sembcorp Utilities is working towards commencing import of electricity from the project by 2035.
"Over the next few years, the consortium will continue to develop the project, including to obtain all requisite approvals from relevant jurisdictions, conclude power purchase agreements with buyers, and secure sufficient financing,” said EMA in a separate statement. - Bernama

articles.full_text:
Partnership aims to connect directors across both countries, promote cross border learning and regionally connected board leaders
SINGAPORE – Media OutReach Newswire – 27 October 2026 – As Singapore and Vietnam deepen their economic ties and more businesses look beyond their home markets for growth, board directors need to understand not only their own businesses but also the opportunities, risks and governance expectations across borders.
Recognising this, the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants (ISCA) and the Vietnam Institute of Corporate Governance (VNICG) are joining forces to build a stronger community of board directors across both countries.
The partnership aims to bring together existing and aspiring board directors from Singapore and Vietnam to exchange knowledge, share practical boardroom experiences and develop the international perspectives needed to guide businesses in an increasingly connected and complex environment.
Connecting boardrooms across borders
ISCA and VNICG will explore opportunities for joint board leadership programmes, professional exchanges and networking activities that connect directors and governance professionals from both countries during this partnership.
The collaboration will draw on the strengths of both organisations: ISCA brings its professional network and experience in board governance, financial oversight and risk management while VNICG contributes its knowledge of Vietnam’s business environment, corporate governance practices and independent director community.
ISCA’s Board of Directors Masterclass, jointly developed by ISCA Academy and SAC Capital, will be incorporated into the Independent Director dual programme, a new initiative jointly developed by ISCA and VNICG. The programme will combine Singapore’s board governance practices with Vietnam’s regulatory and business environment, providing participants with opportunities to learn from both markets.
Beyond formal learning, the partnership seeks to foster lasting professional relationships among directors and encourage greater exchange of ideas on issues such as business strategy, sustainability, emerging technologies and corporate governance.
Strengthening Singapore–Vietnam professional connections
Mr Pang Te Cheng, Consul-General of Singapore in Ho Chi Minh City, said: “Singapore and Vietnam enjoy a strong and comprehensive partnership spanning trade, investment, education, innovation and many other sectors. As Vietnam advances its International Financial Centre ambitions in Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang, alongside discussions at the HCMC Autumn Economic Forum, strengthening corporate governance and professional capabilities will be vital to attracting international capital. I welcome the partnership between ISCA and VNICG, which brings together Singaporean and Vietnamese expertise to enhance professional standards, transparency and investor confidence. Such collaborations can deepen our bilateral ties while supporting Vietnam’s next phase of sustainable economic development.”
Ms Fann Kor, CEO of ISCA, said: “The world is changing rapidly. From geopolitical developments and technological disruption to sustainability, these issues are occupying boardroom conversations. No single market has all the answers. Through our partnership with VNICG, we hope to bring board directors from both Singapore and Vietnam together to exchange knowledge, learn from real experiences and develop the capabilities to navigate an increasingly complex business environment. Our ambition goes beyond training. We want to foster a connected community of internationally minded directors who can learn from one another, ask better questions and make better decisions. When the world enters the boardroom, our judgement must keep pace.”
Mr Hoàng Đức Hùng, President of VNICG, said: “As Vietnamese businesses expand and engage more closely with international investors and partners, our board directors need both strong local knowledge and a wider international perspective. Our partnership with ISCA creates opportunities for Vietnamese directors to exchange experiences with their Singapore counterparts, learn from different governance practices and build valuable professional relationships. We look forward to developing a connected community of directors who can contribute to stronger corporate governance and support the long-term growth of businesses in both countries.”
The partnership was formalised at a signing ceremony held at the Ho Chi Minh Stock Exchange on 27 October 2026.

SINGAPORE: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) must strengthen energy security, accelerate regional electricity connectivity and mobilise investment for energy projects to meet growing demand and improve the region’s resilience, said its Secretary-General Dr Kao Kim Hourn.
He said these three priorities were closely linked and important to translating regional energy cooperation commitments into practical outcomes for member states.
"The priority now is to turn this commitment into practical results," he said in his keynote address at the Singapore International Energy Week (SIEW) Summit here.
Kao said ASEAN must improve its preparedness for energy supply disruptions, diversify its sources of supply and enhance energy efficiency amid uncertainties in global energy markets.
He also stressed the importance of regional cooperation in sharing information, conducting joint emergency exercises and strengthening arrangements to coordinate responses to potential disruptions.
On regional electricity connectivity, Kao said the ASEAN Power Grid could enable countries to share resources, transfer electricity to areas of demand and provide mutual support during supply disruptions.
He said the Laos-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore (LTMS) Power Integration Project had demonstrated that multilateral electricity trade could work, providing a foundation for expanding regional cooperation.
However, he said stronger electricity interconnections would need to be supported by coordinated planning, transparent cross-border trading rules and reliable infrastructure, including arrangements for maintaining and repairing submarine power cables.
Kao also said that governments, private investors and multilateral financial institutions must work together to finance energy infrastructure and ensure regional plans could be translated into deliverable projects.
"I would encourage financial institutions to engage early and remain involved throughout the coordination effort.
"Different projects and stages of development require different forms of financing, grants and support for project operations," he said.
Kao also said governments need to establish clear rules for cross-border electricity trade and fair risk-sharing arrangements to encourage investment.
"Our cooperation will succeed when projects are completed and deliver tangible benefits across the region," said Kao.
In addition, he said Singapore’s ASEAN chairmanship in 2027 would provide an opportunity to advance regional energy commitments and strengthen implementation. - Bernama

The recommendations were made at the CEO 500 program with the theme ‘The Convergence of FDI, Technology and Global Financial Flows,’ held on Monday as part of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, which opened in Ho Chi Minh City on the same day.
Vietnam attracted US$50.36 billion in registered FDI in the first nine months of 2026, up 76.4 percent year on year, according to data presented at the program.
The country also led ASEAN in attracting FDI, according to a 2025 report by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
However, the challenge remains to improve the quality of these inflows, retain more value domestically, and strengthen the capabilities of local businesses.
AI boom heightens need for higher-value FDI
Fazurin Jamaludin, the International Monetary Fund’s resident representative for Vietnam and Laos, said AI is becoming one of the major drivers of global economic growth, particularly in manufacturing, exports, and technology investment.
Despite global economic uncertainties in 2026, including energy shocks and trade-related risks, the global economy has proved more resilient than expected, partly thanks to the AI-driven technology growth cycle, which has boosted demand for hardware production, exports and related services, he said.
In Asia, the AI boom is driving industrial production and intra-regional trade.
Technology investment in the first half of 2026 already exceeded the total for all of 2025, helping several economies grow faster than expected, Jamaludin said.
Vietnam is also benefiting from this growth cycle, although it remains significantly affected by energy shocks.
However, the country’s ability to capitalize on the AI boom would depend on its preparedness, particularly its legal framework, energy infrastructure, and workforce quality, he said.
Jamaludin also warned that if expectations for AI-driven productivity gains and profits fail to materialize, Asia could suffer greater negative impacts than other regions.
For Vietnam and Ho Chi Minh City, he recommended strengthening macroeconomic fundamentals, improving businesses’ access to capital, and modernizing monetary and fiscal policies.
He also stressed the need to improve the quality and transparency of economic data, enabling international investors to better assess Vietnam’s potential and supporting efforts to attract long-term investment.
Nguyen Huu Huan, vice-chairman of the executive agency of the Vietnam International Financial Center in Ho Chi Minh City, said Vietnam needs to change its approach to attracting foreign investment by prioritizing projects that generate greater added value.
The foreign-invested sector has accounted for 80.7 percent of Vietnam’s total export turnover in 2026, but high export figures do not fully reflect domestic technological capabilities or the value retained by Vietnamese businesses, he said.
Vietnam still relies heavily on imported components and materials while undertaking low-value processing and assembly, limiting the value it could generate domestically, Huan said.
The country should invest more in research, design, core technologies, intellectual property, and brand development to increase the value retained by Vietnamese businesses, he added.
Stronger supply chains, industrial infrastructure
From the perspective of foreign investors, Peter James Opdahl, chairman of Singapore-based ITO Group Holdings, said Vietnam needs more extensive and better-connected supply chains to compete with regional economies with well-developed manufacturing ecosystems, such as Japan and South Korea.
The domestic market also needs to be developed to create more business opportunities for small enterprises, particularly those without international customer networks.
Opdahl proposed providing greater support for local businesses to establish partnerships and access global business networks through international networking events.
He also called for continued efforts to improve the investment climate at both central and local levels to make Vietnam more attractive to both foreign and domestic investors.
Beyond institutions and human resources, industrial infrastructure is another important condition for attracting high-tech FDI.
Nguyen The Duy, vice-chairman and deputy general director of Ho Chi Minh City-based Becamex Group, said the city has an opportunity to accelerate development thanks to its expanded development space, interregional infrastructure, and new decentralization mechanisms.
To attract high-tech FDI, Duy proposed transforming traditional industrial parks into green industrial zones, promoting renewable energy through cooperation with the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and working with Singapore’s Advanced Remanufacturing and Technology Center to upgrade automation technology and train highly skilled technical workers.
He also proposed developing a science and technology urban area in northern Ho Chi Minh City that would integrate research, innovation, training, and urban development.

Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan noted that Ho Chi Minh City, along with the rest of the country, continues to make a strong mark in attracting FDI and participating deeply in global supply chains. The foreign-invested sector currently contributes approximately 20.35% of GDP and accounts for over 80% of the country's total export turnover.
However, Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan pointed out a paradox: Currently, foreign value-added in total exports still accounts for 48%, reflecting a high level of dependence on imported raw materials and components. Notably, FDI flows for research and development (R&D) account for only a mere 1.9% of total newly registered FDI; the proportion of highly skilled labor in the manufacturing sector also only reaches about 5%.
"If Vietnam remains merely a low-cost processing and assembly factory, it will struggle to overcome the middle-income trap and face the risk of significant disruption as global trade policies fluctuate," Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan commented.
According to Mr. Huan, these limitations indicate that Vietnam needs to shift from an investment attraction model based on capital scale and production capacity to selecting projects that can generate high added value, promote innovation, and enhance domestic technological capabilities.

Priority areas include artificial intelligence ( AI ) and digital infrastructure, semiconductors, robotics and automation, biotechnology, clean energy, advanced materials, and digital finance. Of these, quantum technology needs to be prepared with a long-term vision.
However, according to Mr. Huan, the selection of priority sectors must be accompanied by identifying stages where Vietnam has the potential to create advantages, such as chip design, AI solution development, component manufacturing, or technology ownership. Capital allocation decisions should also be based on market demand, the quality of human resources, and the potential for spillover effects into the domestic business system.
In this process, the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City (VIFC-HCMC) model is expected to become a "capital injection station" attracting and supplying capital and a "gateway" connecting the new generation of international financial capital with the ecosystem of research institutions, institutes, and technology enterprises.
"FDI capital should not be driven by quantity or total capital, but rather by measuring the quality of the capital flow directed towards core technologies and innovation," he emphasized.
According to the plan shared by Mr. Huan at the CEO500 program, VIFC-HCMC will focus on unlocking three capital flows corresponding to each development stage, including the R&D stage, the commercial stage, and the large-scale production and infrastructure stage.
Based on this orientation, he called on international corporations and investors to work with Ho Chi Minh City to develop future industries. VIFC-HCMC is committed to supporting resource connections and creating favorable conditions for investors to achieve benefits commensurate with their contributions to Vietnam's development.

Therefore, listening directly to the business community is fundamental for the city to assess its own capabilities, leverage its competitive advantages, and remove barriers to capital flows.

First is the area of infrastructure and new development spaces, focusing on transport-oriented development (TOD) urban development projects, seaports, logistics, and free trade zones.

The leaders of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee affirmed the government's stance of engaging in substantive discussions about specific opportunities, support mechanisms and policies, and committing to implementation according to the principle of "clear tasks, clear responsibilities, and clear timelines." With this new mindset, Ho Chi Minh City is not only a large domestic consumer market but is also becoming a strategic gateway connecting Vietnam with global capital, technology, and development resources.
Businesses offer suggestions.

Hanoi (VNA) – Once considered a laggard in attracting investment, Nghe An has emerged as one of Vietnam’s leading destinations for foreign direct investment (FDI). 
The central province attracted more than 108.27 trillion VND (4.18 billion USD) in investment in the first nine months of 2026, including around 2.49 billion USD in FDI – ranking sixth nationwide. 
In 2025, the Nghe An People’s Committee licensed 25 new FDI projects and approved additional investment for 20 existing projects, bringing total newly registered and additional capital to more than 1 billion USD. Several major projects in the Southeast Nghe An Economic Zone became operational, boosting exports and budget revenue while creating jobs and raising local workers’ incomes. 
In 2026, the scale of FDI projects expanded significantly, with billion-dollar projects demonstrating the province’s investment appeal. (NASU). Industry and construction account for 34.05% of the province’s economic structure. 
These figures reflect the continued shift towards industrialisation and modernisation, with manufacturing and FDI enterprises playing an increasingly important role in economic growth and competitiveness. 
Nghe An's economy ranks 14th among Vietnam’s 34 provinces and cities, with industry, particularly manufacturing – processing and surging FDI inflows serving as major growth drivers. Foreign investment has helped expand production capacity, improve technological capabilities and support new industrial value chains, while creating jobs and enhancing the local economy's competitiveness. 
The Nghe An provincial People’s Committee has taken concrete steps to improve the business environment. In late 2025, it approved a plan to simplify administrative procedures under the management of the Southeast Nghe An Economic Zone Management Board. In particular, procedures in the construction sector have been shortened by around 40%. 
Economic experts say that together with available cleared land, an abundant workforce and ongoing infrastructure and logistics projects, streamlined and faster administrative procedures will make the province more attractive to foreign investors. 
Dispong Pornchanoknart, Country Director of WHA in Vietnam, said the company is developing its second industrial park, covering around 250 hectares, as part of its long-term plan to develop approximately 2,000 hectares of industrial parks in Nghe An. Its first industrial park,

After nearly 10 years of operating in the province, the company considers its decision to invest there one of its soundest investment decisions in Vietnam, he said. 
Teng Wei Hong, General Director of VSIP Nghe An Co., Ltd., praised the province for proactively helping investors expand their markets and access orders for high-tech, high-value-added products.

By 2045, the province aims to become a manufacturing, services and innovation hub in central Vietnam, with deeper integration into global value chains. 
The Nghe An provincial master plan for 2021–2030, with a vision to 2050, identifies three strategic breakthroughs in socio-economic development: improving institutions, policies and the business environment; developing human resources linked to science – technology, innovation and digital transformation; and building modern, integrated infrastructure. 
The Southeast Nghe An Economic Zone is designated as the province’s main growth engine, with plans to develop it into a free economic zone focused on industry, logistics, seaports, urban development and the marine economy. 
The recent expansion of the economic zone to 104,000 hectares is expected to help address shortages of industrial land and enable clearer functional zoning. 
Meanwhile, the province is accelerating site clearance for VSIP Nghe An 3, Hoang Mai II and Tho Loc industrial parks. 
Chairman of the Nghe An People’s Committee Vo Trong Hai affirmed that the province will continue building an enabling, action-oriented and service-minded administration, strongly reforming administrative procedures and improving governance to create a transparent, stable and favourable investment environment. It pledges support for businesses throughout the entire project lifecycle, from investment surveys and administrative procedures to site clearance, construction, production, business operations and further expansion./.

articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s four leading e-commerce platforms recorded gross merchandise value (GMV) of VND411.7 trillion ($15.8 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 22% year-on-year, as consumers became more selective amid persistent inflation and rising living costs.
Data from YouNet ECI’s EcomHeat platform showed that GMV across Shopee, TikTok Shop, Lazada and Tiki grew steadily over four consecutive quarters, from Q4/2025 through Q3/2026.
Growth was driven largely by higher selling prices, which increased by over 20% each quarter, while growth in sales volume remained broadly flat.
The trend points to a shift in shopping behavior as consumers weigh product quality and affordability more carefully.
According to YouNet ECI’s eCCI index, 74% of consumers prioritized product quality, up 22 percentage points from Q2/2026. Meanwhile, 67% continued to prioritize price.
Vietnam’s economy expanded 9.95% year-on-year in the third quarter, the fastest pace recorded since the beginning of the year, according to the National Statistics Office. However, consumer price inflation remained a concern, with CPI at 5.1% in Q3.
Retail sales of goods and consumer services totaled more than VND5,900 trillion ($228.3 billion) in the first nine months, up 13.4% from a year earlier. After adjusting for inflation, growth stood at 7.8%, indicating that real purchasing power has not kept pace with the increase in nominal sales revenue.
Average consumer prices rose 4.52% in January-September. Essential expenses, including food, housing, electricity and water, transport and dining out, faced upward price pressure. With a larger share of household income going toward necessities, consumers are increasingly likely to cut back on or postpone non-essential purchases.

The message was conveyed at the 2026 Business Partner Cities (BPC) roundtable held on October 23 in Ho Chi Minh City where Shirley Ng, general manager, International Competitiveness at Australian Industry Group (Ai Group) noted thatreducing emission could become a competitive advantage for businesses.
“In pursuit of this goal, businesses need to assess current emission levels, build a roadmap to adjust production processes and allocate necessary resources aside technology investment, Moreover, the carbon border adjustment mechanism requires businesses to pay closer attention to emissions monitoring and reporting, as well as their ability to meet import markets’ standards,” she said.
| Photo: Lac Nguyen | 
As for small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), limited access to information, funding and resources can increase operating cost, prolong the transition process, as well as hinder them from making effective investment solutions.
Therefore, the challenge is to raise awareness of green production while equipping businesses to meet these requirements in practice.
At the conference, Nguyen Loc Ha, Standing Vice Chairman of Ho Chi Minh City People’s Committee, noted that innovation must be closely linked to commercialisation and business development, while economic growth must go hand in hand with the efficient use of resources.
“These principles also underpin the green transition, requiring environmental solutions to deliver tangible business benefits and be practically implemented,” he said.
In Ho Chi Minh City, emissions reduction efforts are underway across multiple sectors.
Greenhouse gas inventories have been conducted at 360 facilities, of which 240 have developed 2026-2030 emissions reduction plans.
In the transport sector, around 68 per cent of buses run on electricity or other green energy, with the city targeting 100 per cent adoption by early 2027. Additionally, rooftop solar power capacity has reached 1.865,7 MWp.
However, these represent only an initial step for SMEs, as implementation depends on investment capital, technology and production ability.
There must be tailored support resolutions for different business groups, rather than simply prompting them to go green.
To that end, Ho Chi Minh City suggested strengthening market and investor connections, piloting technologies, and fostering collaboration among incubators within the BPC network.
Moriyama Ayako, director general of Economic Strategy Bureau of Osaka city government, said the city is working to put carbon-neutral technologies showcased at World Expo 2025 – a global technology exchange event – into practical use.
“Networking activities such as Vietnam Circular Economy Seminar and Tech Osaka Summit also help link environmental challenges with technology needs, business opportunities and international cooperation,” she said.
Osaka proposed providing SMEs with additional information about environmental challenges and business opportunities in partner cities, integrating green into existing policies and programmes, sharing business-matching events, and strengthening coordination among BPC organisations.
Such measures may help SMEs turn emissions reduction requirements into opportunities, improving production efficiency and maintaining competitiveness.

articles.title: Ho Chi Minh City seeks new value in international investment flows. - Vietnam.vn

Ho Chi Minh City aims to attract projects that bring technology, production capacity, and added value to domestic businesses. Within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, investors proposed that the city prepare infrastructure, improve procedures, and connect resources.
Domestic businesses need to participate more deeply in the value chain.
Within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, Ho Chi Minh City set a requirement to improve the quality of investment attraction. Discussions focused on how to transform international capital into research, production, and innovation capabilities, while expanding opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to participate in supply chains.
Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan, Vice Chairman of the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City (VIFC-HCMC), stated that Vietnam needs to pay more attention to the real value that projects create. The large scale of capital and exports does not fully reflect the technological mastery capacity of domestic enterprises.
Citing figures for the first nine months of 2026, Mr. Huan stated that Vietnam attracted $50.36 billion in registered foreign direct investment (FDI), while implemented capital reached $21.07 billion. The FDI sector continues to make a significant contribution to production and exports, but the economy remains considerably dependent on imported raw materials and components.
According to OECD data cited by Mr. Huan at the program, in 2020, foreign-sourced value-added accounted for approximately 48% of Vietnam's export value. Domestic value accounted for about 52%, including contributions from FDI enterprises operating in Vietnam. Therefore, Vietnam needs to develop research, design, core technologies, intellectual property, and brands.
Mr. Huan proposed that VIFC-HCMC become the focal point for directing international capital into high value-added industries. Priority areas include AI , semiconductors, automation, robotics, digital technology, digital finance, biotechnology, and green technology.
According to him, each project needs to link investment with research, engineer training, technology transfer, and the development of domestic suppliers. The effectiveness of attracting FDI must be demonstrated through the new capabilities of the economy, in addition to the registered and disbursed capital.
Mr. Peter James Opdahl, Chairman of ITO Group Holdings, stated that Vietnam has become a strategic manufacturing hub for the group in the field of industrial automation since 2012. The company is implementing a plan for a new factory with an area of approximately 12,000 m² under the Green Channel mechanism.
Based on his investment experience, Mr. Opdahl suggested that Vietnam continue to develop supporting industries, assisting small and medium-sized enterprises in participating in global production networks. All parties need to strengthen engineering training, technology transfer, and enhance the research, design, and production capabilities of domestic enterprises.
Mr. Nguyen The Duy, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors and Deputy General Director of Becamex Group, noted that the new generation of investors are interested in connectivity infrastructure, technology, human resources, and support services. Becamex is developing smart, eco-friendly industrial parks that link production with research, automation, and training.
The business aims to develop the Science and Technology Urban Area in the North of Ho Chi Minh City into an integrated ecosystem of high-tech industries, research, innovation, and a modern urban environment. Mr. Duy suggested that the city continue to build breakthrough mechanisms to attract projects with high added value.

In the aviation sector, Mr. To Viet Thang, Permanent Deputy General Director and Chief Safety Officer of Vietjet , believes that Long Thanh International Airport opens up more opportunities for the development of the aviation industry, logistics, and support services. He emphasized the need to apply AI, big data, digitize operations, and prepare high-quality human resources, linking technological innovation with green development.
The proposal needs to be transformed into a feasible project .
Collaborative opportunities can only become projects when investors see clear implementation conditions. Businesses in the CEO500 list are interested in infrastructure connectivity, policy predictability, and coordination mechanisms between agencies.
Nick Chong, Head of Investment Advisory for Southeast Asia at Arup Group, argues that infrastructure creates economic value through connectivity. Investors evaluate the overall transportation corridor, logistics, industrial parks, innovation centers, and urban areas connected to public transport, rather than considering individual projects.
According to Mr. Chong, international funding prioritizes projects with feasible implementation plans, transparent information, and clear risk allocation mechanisms. The government needs to link infrastructure development with land use planning, industry, finance, and the ability to mobilize private capital. He also suggested that all parties define responsibilities and implementation mechanisms from the preparation stage. The government, businesses, and development finance institutions need to cooperate to translate infrastructure needs into projects capable of attracting investment.
Mr. Marc Knapper, former US Ambassador to Vietnam, Chairman of Knapper Global Advisors, and Advisor to VIFC-HCMC, emphasized three requirements of investors: clear and responsive points of contact; transparent procedures with predictable deadlines; and stable and consistent policies.
According to Mr. Knapper, many high-quality projects have implementation periods ranging from 5 to 20 years, and the predictability of policies therefore directly impacts investment decisions. The city needs to quickly develop a list of priority projects, expand international financial services, and establish a one-stop mechanism to support investors.
Mr. Ge Jun, CEO of TOJOY Enterprise Services, introduced the strategic direction for promoting a portfolio of five projects in Ho Chi Minh City, focusing on AI, clean energy, construction robotics, and the low-income economy.
TOJOY representatives proposed establishing a cooperation mechanism with the Global Sharing Office within the next 60–90 days. The parties will continue working to clarify the implementation conditions, aiming to transform the exchanges into a feasible project.
Mr. Nguyen Cong Vinh, Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, stated that the value of activities within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum lies in its ability to transform connections into cooperation, ideas into initiatives, and commitments into concrete projects. The city is ready to cooperate in identifying locations, resources, conditions, and timelines for feasible proposals.
In addition, the City has assigned the Center for the Fourth Industrial Revolution in Ho Chi Minh City as the focal point for compiling recommendations, proposals, and projects from the program. The Center will coordinate with relevant agencies to continue working with businesses and investors after the forum.
Mr. Nguyen Cong Vinh also encouraged large corporations to strengthen links with domestic businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises. These links should promote technology transfer, human resource training, and enhance participation in global value chains.

articles.summary: Ho Chi Minh City: Connecting new advantages to create momentum for growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City is transforming with the convergence of capital and technology. Discover how the city is enhancing its position in the global value chain.
The Autumn Economic Forum's (AEF) CEO 500 program (October 26-29) is expected to bring together over 500 domestic and international business leaders, focusing on the convergence of FDI, technology, and global financial flows. For the city, this is an opportunity to engage in dialogue with key stakeholders who determine investment locations, supply chains, and markets. The crucial question is: what challenges can Ho Chi Minh City help them solve?
Globalization is changing the way we operate. Besides costs, businesses must consider supply chain security, trade policies, access to technology, and environmental standards.
The WTO's March 2026 trade report highlights the risk of prolonged conflict increasing fuel and transportation costs and disrupting trade routes. Therefore, attracting investment opportunities must be coupled with the requirement to establish a reliable production and business location.
Following its merger with Binh Duong and Ba Ria - Vung Tau , Ho Chi Minh City is in a position to combine knowledge-based services, finance, industrial infrastructure, and the Cai Mep - Thi Vai deep-water port.Within the geographical area connecting the Southeast region with the Mekong Delta and the international market, the city can organize design, supply, production, and export services. This is a geoeconomic advantage that needs to be transformed into competitiveness.
However, being a gateway location does not guarantee a high position in the value chain. An export container may contain a large proportion of imported raw materials; a high-tech project may have few connections with domestic suppliers.
Additional metrics that need to be considered are value created locally, orders for Vietnamese businesses, and accumulated technical capabilities. The scale of trade only becomes a strength when it nurtures the underlying production.
Openness also increases the potential for shock transmission. Changes in tariffs, rules of origin, or technology controls can simultaneously impact orders, capital flows, and jobs. Cities need to support businesses in diversifying their customers and supply sources; improving their traceability and market compliance capabilities. International connectivity must be accompanied by the ability to detect risks early and maintain operations when a link is disrupted.
You may also like
Reorganize the space to reduce connectivity costs.
The bottleneck that needs to be addressed is operational fragmentation. Unified boundaries need to be followed by interconnected planning, data, procedures, and investments. If projects remain entangled between multiple points of contact, and goods continue to be delayed at various junctions, the benefits of consolidation will be eroded by coordination costs. International investors evaluate locations based on their daily operational experience.
A multi-centered network should be organized according to complementary functions. The central area should develop high-value services; industrial areas should promote advanced manufacturing and supporting industries; and port areas should be linked to logistics and maritime services.
Planning must ensure that land for production, housing, public services, and public transportation develop together, avoiding pushing workers away from job opportunities.
Infrastructure should be selected based on its ability to improve the overall network efficiency. Port connections must be synchronized with interchanges, warehouses, waterways, and digital procedures. For businesses participating in international supply chains, consistent delivery times can determine their ability to retain orders. Therefore, investment efficiency should be measured by time, cost, and transportation reliability.
Linking with Dong Nai , Tay Ninh, and the Mekong Delta requires joint projects, a coordinating body, specific funding, and timelines. Seaports need cargo; industries need suppliers; and urban areas need water and ecological space. Competing to attract projects through individual incentives easily undermines the common good. The city must work with localities to build economic corridors capable of serving a broader market.
Mobilizing international resources also requires professional project preparation. The site, financial plan, technical standards, and risk-bearing parties must be identified in advance. Public funds should focus on removing bottlenecks that pave the way for private investment; public-private partnerships need transparent budgetary obligations. International partners must see an opportunity that is feasible and verifiable.
Retain capabilities from each investment project.
You may also like
In the first nine months of 2026, the city's GRDP increased by 9.06%. To achieve and maintain double-digit growth, it is necessary to combine the release of currently stagnant resources with long-term productivity enhancement. Expanding space creates more favorable conditions; growth must come from more efficient use of capital, labor, and technology.
The priority is to transform FDI attraction into a process of enhancing the capacity of domestic businesses. It is necessary to organize supplier development programs based on specific purchasing needs, support quality certification, provide technical training, and connect research. Trade linkages that can be sustained by business efficiency will create a sustainable foundation for knowledge transfer.
Technology collaboration needs to start with real-world problems. AI can support quality control, demand forecasting, and transportation optimization; universities and research institutes need to engage with businesses from the problem-solving stage. Cities can leverage connections with the WEF and the C4IR network to find partners, access technology management expertise, and then transform it into a funded program with application and productivity metrics.
Green transformation needs to be organized into market access capabilities: emission measurement, energy efficiency, traceability, and data verification. Shared support in consulting, testing, and data will help small businesses meet standards at a reasonable cost. Stable electricity, data security, flood control, and quality of life must also be considered fundamental to attracting investment and talent.
Following the forum, each commitment needs a project, a responsible person, and implementation milestones. Success must be identified through operational capital, applied technology, and Vietnamese businesses gaining greater capacity to participate in international supply chains. When internal capabilities are strong enough to transform external opportunities, Ho Chi Minh City will have the impetus to elevate its regional standing, while simultaneously creating further impetus for national development.
MAJOR GENERAL, ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR, DR. TRAN TRUNG TIN - FORMER DIRECTOR OF THE ECONOMIC DEPARTMENT, MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE

(Hochiminhcity.gov.vn) - “VIFC-HCMC needs to become a coordinating body for development, connecting and directing international capital into high value-added industries. The capital flow must help Vietnam master technology, create a leap in productivity, and build businesses capable of competing globally,” stated Assoc. Prof. Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan, Vice Chairman of the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City, at the Autumn Economic Forum held on the afternoon of October 26th.
VIFC-HCMC should be the channel for coordinating capital flows.
According to Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan, in the first nine months of 2026, registered foreign investment reached US$50.36 billion, while implemented FDI reached US$21.07 billion. This result needs to be viewed in conjunction with the export structure and domestic technological capacity.
First, there is the level of dependence on the FDI sector in exports. Of the total export value of goods worth US$434.30 billion in the first nine months of 2026, the FDI sector, including crude oil, contributed US$350.41 billion, equivalent to 80.7%. The domestic economic sector accounted for only 19.3%. This means that for every US$100 worth of goods exported, more than US$80 was generated by the FDI sector.
From this structure, it is clear that the economy relies heavily on the FDI sector, particularly in the export sector. The export capacity of domestic enterprises is not yet commensurate. When international corporations change orders, markets, or production locations, our export growth and employment will be affected. Therefore, improving the capacity of Vietnamese enterprises is essential for the resilience of the economy.

Mr. Huan also informed that, according to the OECD report in 2026, in newly announced FDI projects during the 2020-2024 period, research and development activities accounted for only about 1.9% of the total investment capital. The World Bank's Vietnam 2045 report, published in 2024, also showed that only about 5% of the workforce in the processing and manufacturing sector belonged to the high-skilled group.
These data reinforce the view that Vietnam's export model is still heavily reliant on processing and assembly, while its research and innovation capabilities have not developed proportionally. A high-tech export economy needs to continue to improve its design capabilities and master core technologies locally.
Therefore, we need to attract a new generation of capital linked to research and development, engineering training, technological cooperation, and upgrading Vietnamese suppliers. This capital must help Vietnamese businesses gradually participate more deeply in high value-added stages, create intellectual property, and enhance their position in the global value chain. This is the requirement for Ho Chi Minh City and VIFC-HCMC.
Mr. Huan stated that VIFC-HCMC should not only be a channel for capital flow, but should also become a coordinating body to ensure that capital contributes to changing the structure and capacity of the economy.
That role begins with translating national development priorities into a portfolio of projects capable of attracting investment. The center needs to coordinate with ministries, departments, localities, universities, and businesses to identify high-value sectors, pinpoint technology gaps, and connect them with suitable investors.
Funding for research must be linked to experts and laboratories. Funding for commercialization needs to be linked to customers and markets. Funding for production must support the formation of supply chains in Vietnam. Good coordination will help resources complement each other and create capabilities that individual projects would find difficult to develop on their own.

This orientation aligns with Resolution 57-NQ/TW, which emphasizes that science, technology, innovation, and digital transformation play a key role as the driving force of development. VIFC-HCMC needs to help connect this orientation with resources and specific projects, following market principles and within the legal framework.
Opportunities to attract international capital through VIFC-HCMC
Reflecting on the investor's perspective, Marc Knapper, former US Ambassador to Vietnam and Chairman of Knapper Global (KGA), stated that the narrative among global investors has changed. A few years ago, they were asking whether or not to invest in Vietnam. Now, their question is how to invest, and how quickly. Capital is currently flowing into manufacturing, semiconductors, energy, and infrastructure. These investors increasingly want to finance, hedge against risks, and manage that capital within Vietnam, rather than from Singapore or Hong Kong. VIFC-HCM can provide them with that platform.
To attract investors through VIFC-HCM, Marc Knapper suggested that, in terms of developing financial services, global investors need services such as trade finance, hedging, foreign exchange accounts, custody, and cross-border payments that operate smoothly through VIFC-HCM, similar to those in Singapore or Tokyo. Involving international investors in early discussions will help ensure that these services are built around the very people who will use them.
Regarding international fundraising, Marc Knapper believes that investors make decisions most quickly when they can see a concrete project portfolio. With a list of priority projects in the energy, infrastructure, and green transition sectors, ready to welcome international participation and funding through VIFC-HCM, interest will be transformed into concrete commitments.
We also hope the City will promote the issuance of bonds through VIFC-HCM, including green bonds and infrastructure bonds from the City as well as leading Vietnamese businesses. This will help international investors access a familiar and direct channel to contribute capital to the City's growth.
Regarding connecting with global financial institutions, Mr. Marc Knapper stated that many leading banks, insurance companies, and asset managers in Tokyo, Seoul, and New York are still largely unaware of VIFC-HCM. KGA is ready to cooperate with the City to reach these partners and support inviting their influential leaders to Ho Chi Minh City to directly explore the opportunities.
The Chairman of Knapper Global stated that, to realize these opportunities, the City must meet requirements such as: a single point of contact and rapid response; clear regulations and roadmaps for licensing, land, and permit procedures; and consistency, so that decisions made today remain valid tomorrow.
In addition, the city needs to apply streamlined procedures for priority projects and boldly apply special mechanisms for public-private partnership (PPP) projects and projects attracting international capital.
Furthermore, the City is building a professional workforce at VIFC-HCM, including both Vietnamese and international experts. Investors should know that when they work with VIFC-HCM, they are interacting with experts who understand their business sector.
Emphasis should be placed on technological development.
Meanwhile, Don Lam, Director and Founding Shareholder of VinaCapital, suggested that, in addition to green bonds and municipal bonds already discussed by financial experts, investment managers and banks should consider other ways to bring capital to Vietnamese businesses that are in dire need of international funding to support their growth.

The current demand for capital is enormous, and an increasing amount of capital is flowing into the technology sector. Technology will be one of the key drivers of Vietnam's growth in the coming years.
If Vietnam wants to overcome the middle-income trap and move towards becoming a developed country by 2045, it needs to focus on technological development.
Mr. Don Lam stated that VietCapital has been working with numerous technology companies and venture capital funds, connecting these entities with Ho Chi Minh City. We also collaborate with US-based technology companies to attract investment and develop research and development (R&D) centers in the city.
VietCapital is also aiming to develop a venture capital and startup ecosystem, including Vietnamese startups based on technological capabilities. One initiative mentioned is the Robotics Innovation Hub at BISC, where technology companies can establish operations and access the benefits of this ecosystem. This will open up significant opportunities for international investors to participate in the Vietnamese stock market, while also attracting more long-term international investment flows.
Recently, VietCapital continued to hold its annual investor conference in Ho Chi Minh City. One of the key issues was that Vietnam is being recognized as an emerging market by FTSE Russell.
Mr. Don Lam expects that by the end of 2027, Vietnam could be included in the MSCI indices, and affirmed that VietCapital will continue to contribute to the development of Vietnam's capital market.
