Tokenizing ETDs connects PrimeRevenue's global network of funding partners directly to on-chain capital markets. The ambition is to extend access to eligible on-chain investors over time.
Beyond ETDs, PrimeRevenue sees potential to bring a wider range of working capital instruments on-chain, giving corporates new ways to unlock liquidity and giving its network of funders access to a high-quality, short-duration real-world asset class.
ETDs represent a buyer's obligation to pay a specified amount at a defined future date. PrimeRevenue's technology already manages these instruments electronically. Moving them on-chain with Solana maximizes the potential for zero-friction reconciliation. Each issuance, transfer, lifecycle event and maturity settlement is captured instantly so capital can move at the pace of commerce on a verifiable, shared record.
PrimeRevenue brings unrivaled scale to this move: a global working capital platform used by 50,000 companies, supported by over 100 funding partners and facilitating more than $300 billion in annual payment transactions. The initiative puts corporate payment obligations from an established global network on-chain and connects them with new sources of institutional capital.
Solana combines fast, low-cost transactions with a growing ecosystem of institutional investors, asset managers and tokenized asset providers. This gives PrimeRevenue the infrastructure and market connections to distribute ETDs to a broader range of financial institutions, and to scale to further asset types as the program grows.
PJ Bain, CEO, PrimeRevenue, commented:
"PrimeRevenue has spent more than two decades building the world's leading working capital network. Now we are taking it on-chain. Bringing Electronic Time Drafts to Solana is the first step in moving traditional trade finance onto infrastructure that is transparent by design, settles in seconds and is accessible to capital anywhere in the world. This is about far more than a single instrument. It creates new pathways to unlock working capital and liquidity for our customers and funding partners."

articles.title: Ho Chi Minh City pitches infrastructure, finance, energy, tech to global investors - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Ho Chi Minh City pitches infrastructure, finance, energy, tech to global investors  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) - Ho Chi Minh City is staking its next phase of growth on infrastructure, finance, energy and digital economy, heard the CEO 500 Programme themed "Convergence of FDI, technology and global financial flows", part of the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum, on October 26.
Linking capital flows with four new growth drivers
Nguyen Cong Vinh, Vice Chairman of the municipal People’s Committee, said the dialogue is meant to do more than raise funds. The city wants to work with investors to pinpoint new opportunities, solve specific development problems and build growth momentum as technology advances quickly and global capital shifts.
According to him, the merger with Binh Duong and Ba Ria-Vung Tau has enlarged the city’s economic and urban footprint, giving it more room for large-scale projects. New policies, including the Politburo’s Resolution 10-NQ/TW on foreign-invested sector development, Resolution 19-NQ/TW dated July 28, 2026 on renewing Vietnam’s growth model, and the Urban Development Law, should let the city step up decentralisation and delegation of authority in planning and resource mobilisation.
Competing for global capital, the city is targeting quality FDI in finance, technology, digital transformation, green economy, sustainable development and innovation. It aims to draw 19 billion USD in FDI in 2026, he said.
The city has set four priority areas for talks with the business community. In infrastructure, it is pushing transit-oriented development (TOD), seaports, logistics and free trade zones, which can widen its economic footprint, improve connectivity and support production and trade.
In finance, the city wants the Vietnam International Financial Centre (VIFC) in Ho Chi Minh City to become a conduit to regional capital and markets. It is asking global financial institutions to join from the outset and help define conditions, procedures and an operating roadmap.
In energy, reliable clean power is increasingly a prerequisite for urban, industrial and logistics projects. The city wants investors to settle on the right models, priority areas and rollout timelines.
In the digital economy and technology, Ho Chi Minh City is focusing on data infrastructure, artificial intelligence, high-tech zones and a regulatory sandbox where companies can test, deploy and scale technology solutions.
Vinh said the city expects substantive discussions on investment opportunities, funding needs, support mechanisms and timelines. Proposals made at the programme should become projects, initiatives and partnerships that can actually be delivered, with clear tasks, roles and timelines.
It also wants to serve as Vietnam’s gateway to global and regional capital, technology, markets and resources. That will let companies tap the domestic market, link up with manufacturing, logistics, finance and technology hubs, and expand across the region, he added.
Investors flag workforce, supply chain gaps
Nick Chong, Southeast Asia Investor Advisory Leader at Arup Group, said the Government must invest in a workforce suited to advanced manufacturing and innovative industries. That would help Vietnam move up the value chain and attract more high-tech projects.
Coordinated planning and network-style infrastructure will help companies scale up production. Projects still need to be economically viable, able to attract capital and structured with clearly defined roles for each stakeholder, he said.
Peter James Opdahl, President of ITO Group Holdings, said the “green lane” investment mechanism has given companies the framework they need to move faster and bring new factories online.
Even so, he said Vietnam needs deeper supply chains to compete with long-established industrial economies such as Japan, the Republic of Korea and China. A stronger domestic market will also open opportunities, especially for small companies with limited experience and market access abroad.
Vietnam needs about 1.4 trillion USD in infrastructure investment through 2045. Meeting that will take the public and private sectors and international financial institutions together, said Don Lam, CEO and Founding Partner of VinaCapital.
With Vietnam targeting annual economic growth of 8-10%, he said the VIFC could help financial organisations find investment opportunities and channel global capital into infrastructure and domestic development./.

articles.title: Despite tens of billions of USD in foreign investment, Vietnam is still struggling with the problem of increasing added value. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Despite tens of billions of USD in foreign investment, Vietnam is still struggling with the problem of increasing added value.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan believes that the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City needs to play a coordinating role in channeling international capital into high value-added industries, contributing to enhancing the technological capacity and competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses.
Linking capital flows with technological capabilities.
At the CEO 500 program themed "The Convergence of FDI, Technology, and Global Financial Flows" within the framework of the Autumn Economic Forum 2026, held on the afternoon of October 26th, Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Huu Huan, Vice Chairman of the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City, emphasized the need to change the approach in attracting foreign investment. Accordingly, capital flows should not only serve to expand production but also contribute to helping Vietnam master technology, increase productivity, and form businesses capable of competing in the global market.
According to Mr. Huan, the Vietnam International Finance Center in Ho Chi Minh City (VIFC-HCMC) needs to become a hub connecting and directing international capital into high value-added sectors. This is not just about attracting more financial resources, but also about upgrading the growth model and increasing the participation of domestic businesses in key stages of the global value chain.
To clarify the need for innovation in the investment attraction model, Mr. Huan cited figures showing that the scale of foreign capital inflows into Vietnam continues to be large. In the first nine months of 2026, registered foreign investment reached US$50.36 billion, while implemented FDI reached US$21.07 billion.
However, according to Mr. Huan, these figures should be considered in conjunction with the export structure and domestic technological capabilities to more fully assess the effectiveness of investment flows.
In the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam's total merchandise exports reached US$434.30 billion. Of this, the foreign-invested sector, including crude oil, contributed US$350.41 billion, equivalent to 80.7%; the domestic economic sector accounted for 19.3%.
Mr. Huan emphasized that developing high-tech human resources requires coordination between universities, research institutes, and businesses. VIFC-HCMC is expected to connect capital with training, attract experts, and foster international cooperation, helping Vietnamese businesses gradually adopt, master, and innovate technology, enhance design capabilities, intellectual property, and their position in the global supply chain.
Mr. Huan cited the OECD report from 2026, according to which research and development activities accounted for only about 1.9% of the total investment in newly announced FDI projects during the 2020-2024 period.
You may also like
According to Mr. Huan, these data highlight the need to attract investment linked to research and development, engineering training, technological cooperation, and upgrading domestic supplier systems. The goal is not only to increase investment scale but also to create conditions for Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in high-value stages of the global production chain.
Shaping high-value technology industries
Based on the above situation, Mr. Huan believes that VIFC-HCMC needs to assume a broader role than just a capital channel. The center is expected to become a focal point for coordinating and connecting financial resources with development priorities and the need to upgrade the capacity of the economy.
Following this direction, VIFC-HCMC needs to coordinate with ministries, departments, localities, universities, research institutes, and businesses to identify areas with high value-added potential, pinpoint technological gaps, and connect with suitable investors.
Funding mobilization needs to be linked to supporting conditions. Funding for research must be accompanied by experts and laboratories; funding for commercialization needs to be linked to customers and markets; while investment in production needs to support the formation of supply chains in Vietnam.
According to Mr. Huan, when resources are connected synchronously, the impact of capital flows can extend beyond the scope of a single project, contributing to the formation of production and technological capacity for an entire industry group.
The areas mentioned by Mr. Huan include artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure, semiconductors, robotics and automation, biotechnology, clean energy, advanced materials, and digital finance. Quantum technology is also included in the long-term planning vision.
However, attracting investment in these areas needs to be accompanied by specific choices regarding the technological areas in which Vietnam has the capacity to develop, such as chip design, artificial intelligence solution development, component manufacturing, or technology ownership.
You may also like
For each project, effectiveness lies not only in the amount of capital raised but also in its ability to create advancements in business capacity, develop a team of experts, commercialize products, and increase the rate of domestic added value.
According to Mr. Huan, VIFC-HCMC needs to connect international capital flows with high value-added industries, while linking investment with the development of technology, human resources, research, and domestic supply chains. Investment efficiency should be evaluated through productivity, mastered technology, commercialized products, and domestic added value. This is the direction to enhance the capacity of Vietnamese businesses, create long-term growth momentum, and increase global competitiveness, aiming to become a developed, high-income country by 2045.
Ho Chi Minh City shifts its growth strategy, making technology the cornerstone.
Ho Chi Minh City is strengthening the connection between research and production, promoting the fields of artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and green industries, aiming to build a new generation industrial city after the merger.

articles.title: Vietnam-EU bilateral trade volume is heading towards the $100 billion mark. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam-EU bilateral trade volume is heading towards the $100 billion mark.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Vietnamese goods are increasing their presence in the EU market. (Pictured: Vietnam's seafood exports to the EU from the beginning of the year to date reached US$1.4 billion, an increase of 12.6%). | 
 Vietnamese goods are increasing their presence in the EU.
 Geopolitical conflicts and ongoing fighting in the Middle East since the end of February, along with rising energy prices, are putting pressure on the cost of living and purchasing power in many countries, including EU nations. Despite this, Vietnamese exports to this market continue to maintain positive growth.
 According to data from the General Statistics Office ( Ministry of Finance ), in the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam's exports to the EU reached US$50.7 billion, an increase of 21.7% compared to the same period last year. Conversely, the EU exported nearly US$15 billion worth of goods to Vietnam, mainly machinery, equipment, pharmaceuticals, transport vehicles and spare parts.
 Total bilateral trade turnover in the past nine months reached approximately US$65.6 billion, further demonstrating the resilience of Vietnam-EU trade relations amidst global economic uncertainties. 
 Promoting Vietnam-EU relations At the invitation of His Majesty King Frederik X and Queen of Denmark, President of the European Council António Costa, and Prime Minister of Belgium Bart De Wever, General Secretary and President To Lam, along with his wife and a high-level Vietnamese delegation, paid a State visit to the Kingdom of Denmark, an official visit to the European Union, and the Kingdom of Belgium from October 19-24, 2026. According to EU Ambassador to Vietnam Julien Guerrier, the visit of General Secretary and President To Lam to the EU is an important milestone, creating momentum to promote the Vietnam-EU relationship to develop more deeply, substantively, and effectively.  One of the key drivers of bilateral trade is the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA). Signed in June 2019 and officially effective from August 1, 2020, the agreement creates tariff advantages, expands market access opportunities, and encourages businesses from both sides to participate more deeply in supply chains.
 The Ministry of Industry and Trade assesses that, among the 17 free trade agreements that Vietnam is currently implementing, the EVFTA offers significant advantages, as evidenced by Vietnam maintaining a large trade surplus with the EU.
 The agreement has played a positive role in maintaining and promoting trade growth between Vietnam and the 27 EU member states. Despite the instability in the regional market and the challenges facing the EU supply chain and economy, Vietnam's exports have maintained high growth rates, demonstrating the improving supply capacity and adaptability of domestic businesses.
 In 2025, the total value of Vietnam-EU merchandise trade is projected to reach over US$73.8 billion, an increase of 7.8% compared to 2024. Of this, Vietnam's exports to the EU are expected to reach nearly US$56.2 billion, an increase of 8.6%, accounting for 11.8% of the country's total merchandise exports.
 Notably, Vietnam continues to maintain a large trade surplus with the EU, reaching over $38.5 billion in 2025, higher than the $35 billion of the previous year.
 The main export product groups all recorded positive results. In 2025, computers, electronic products and components led with a turnover of US$9.8 billion, an increase of 12.4% compared to 2024. This was followed by machinery, equipment, tools and spare parts at US$7.1 billion, an increase of 1.3%; and telephones and components at US$6.8 billion, an increase of 9.7%. These three product groups accounted for approximately 42% of Vietnam's total export turnover to the EU.
 In addition, footwear exports reached $6 billion, an increase of 4.8%; textiles and garments reached $4.7 billion, an increase of 11.2%; and handbags, wallets, suitcases, hats, and umbrellas reached $1 billion, an increase of 4.4%.
 These results show that Vietnamese businesses are gradually adapting to the increasingly stringent EU requirements regarding technical standards, labor, and sustainable development. The EU continues to be an important market for Vietnamese industrial and consumer goods.
 For Hung Yen Garment Corporation, the EU is a traditional market and continues to be a focus for the company in order to increase exports. According to Mr. Chu Huu Nghi, Deputy General Director of Hung Yen Garment Corporation, the EVFTA creates more room for Vietnamese goods to accelerate exports, but at the same time places high demands on compliance. This requires businesses to constantly upgrade their production and management capabilities to meet market standards.
 Besides industrial goods, many agricultural products also recorded significant growth. In 2025, coffee exports to the EU reached US$3.6 billion, an increase of 68.3% in value and 26.1% in volume. This result reflects the combined impact of rising world coffee prices and the potential for expanding market share of Vietnamese coffee thanks to improved quality, enhanced deep processing, and traceability.
 Exports of fruits and vegetables increased by 45.7%, reaching $353 million; cashew nuts reached $1.05 billion, up 25.2%; and seafood reached $1.4 billion, up 12.6%. These items continue to record positive results, showing the potential for expanding exports to the EU.
 These developments show that opportunities to increase market share in the EU lie not only in traditional export product groups, but also in sectors that can better meet requirements for quality, food safety, and sustainability.
 Expanding bilateral trade opportunities.
 Vietnam-EU relations continue to be strengthened as the two sides upgrade to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in January 2026, coinciding with the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations. This new cooperation framework creates a favorable political foundation for both sides to expand cooperation in many areas, including trade, technology, and green growth.
 The European Union Ambassador to Vietnam, Julien Guerrier, emphasized that the Vietnam-EU relationship is developing steadily, comprehensively, and increasingly deeply, encompassing almost all areas.
 Meanwhile, the Vietnamese Ambassador to the Kingdom of Belgium and Head of the Vietnamese Delegation to the EU, Nguyen Huong Tra, stated that Vietnam-EU relations are currently in a positive phase of development. Political trust between the two sides is constantly being strengthened through high-level exchanges and contacts. Vietnam continues to be the EU's largest trading partner in ASEAN, while the EU is one of Vietnam's four largest trading partners.
 “Both sides are implementing the signed agreements and commitments more effectively; leveraging each side’s strengths to increase complementarity in cooperation, with Vietnam wishing to further strengthen cooperation in science and technology, innovation, and digital transformation with the EU. Vietnam also expects to play a larger role in bridging cooperation between the EU and ASEAN in general and each ASEAN member in particular,” said Ms. Nguyen Huong Tra.
 With its large market size, the EU still has ample room for Vietnamese goods to increase their presence. The bloc imports approximately €2.5 trillion worth of goods annually; including intra-bloc trade, the total reaches €4.025 trillion. Although Vietnam's exports to the EU are growing positively, its market share in this market is still only slightly over 2%.
 Looking at individual member markets, Vietnam's exports are concentrated in the Netherlands, reaching US$13.5 billion; Germany at US$9.53 billion; Italy at US$5.3 billion; Spain at US$4.12 billion; and Belgium at US$3.58 billion. Meanwhile, export turnover to some markets remains quite modest, such as Luxembourg at US$110 million, Croatia at US$77 million, Romania at US$404 million, and Denmark at US$426 million.
 This indicates that there is still significant room for market expansion within the EU. However, it is also a demanding market, with increasingly high standards for quality, environment, labor, and traceability. To effectively capitalize on these opportunities, Vietnamese businesses need to shift from competing primarily on price to improving quality, meeting standards, and increasing the added value of their products.
 The Department of Foreign Market Development and Multilateral Trade (Ministry of Industry and Trade) recommends that, in the coming period, to more effectively exploit the EVFTA, Vietnamese businesses need to accelerate production transformation, focusing on green growth and sustainable development criteria, and meeting EU import standards for both industrial and agricultural/fishery products.
 Entering its seventh year of implementation, the EU's tariff reduction roadmap for Vietnamese goods is nearing completion, expanding market access opportunities for domestic manufacturers. Conversely, Vietnam's tariff reduction process for EU goods also facilitates easier access to European products for domestic consumers.

articles.title: VEFTA Agreement: Expanding markets and attracting high-quality investment from Europe. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: VEFTA Agreement: Expanding markets and attracting high-quality investment from Europe.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In the context of volatile global trade, VEFTA not only opens up more opportunities to access markets in Europe but also helps Vietnam attract high-quality capital and advanced technology.
In the context of a volatile global trade environment, the signing of the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA) is significant.This not only opens up more opportunities to access developed markets in Europe but also creates momentum for Vietnamese businesses to enhance their competitiveness and participate more deeply in the global value chain.
Expanding markets and enhancing position in the value chain.
The European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Switzerland, Norway , Iceland, and Liechtenstein, are economies with strengths in technology, finance, and innovation, and are not members of the European Union (EU). Therefore, VEFTA adds a new cooperation framework to Vietnam's integration network in Europe.
In the context of a volatile global trade environment, VEFTA not only opens up more opportunities to access developed markets in Europe but also creates momentum for Vietnamese businesses to enhance their competitiveness. The agreement covers trade in goods, services, investment, intellectual property, dispute resolution, trade and sustainable development.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade , the average annual trade turnover between Vietnam and EFTA is approximately 2 billion USD. Vietnam mainly exports seafood, footwear, textiles, and electronic equipment; while importing machinery, industrial equipment, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals.
Speaking at the Switzerland-Vietnam Economic Forum Hanoi 2026, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung said that tariff preferences will help Vietnamese goods expand their markets and enhance their competitiveness; while also creating conditions for EFTA businesses to exploit the potential of the Vietnamese market.
Rules of origin also facilitate production linkages and supply chain connections between Europe and Southeast Asia. “In the context of a still uncertain global economy, the Agreement establishes a transparent, stable, and predictable cooperation framework, helping businesses feel secure in making long-term investments,” the Minister emphasized.
For the fisheries sector, opportunities lie not only in exports but also in cooperation in exploitation, processing, and technology application. Ms. Le Hang, Deputy Secretary General of the Vietnam Association of Seafood Processing and Export (VASEP), believes that VEFTA can help businesses enhance their competitiveness and participate more deeply in the global seafood value chain.
According to Vietnam Customs, in the first nine months of 2026, seafood exports to Switzerland reached over $25 million, a decrease of 10%; and to Norway reached $12 million, a decrease of 5% compared to the same period. In this context, the VEFTA is expected to create further impetus for exploiting these markets, especially for high value-added products.
You may also like
The experience of the timber industry in the EU also demonstrates the importance of market diversification. Mr. Ngo Sy Hoai, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Timber and Forest Products Association (VIFOREST), said that timber exports to the EU this year increased by about 25-30%, helping to offset the decline in the US market due to the impact of reciprocal tariffs.
According to Mr. Hoai, successful exports to the EU also affirm the ability of businesses to meet stringent standards, including the requirement not to cause deforestation and forest degradation as stipulated in the EUDR. The recently signed VEFTA agreement will certainly increase the purchasing power for Vietnamese wood products in this market.
On the investment side, VEFTA is expected to help Vietnam attract high-quality capital, advanced technology, and management expertise. Many EFTA corporations are already present in Vietnam in the industrial, food, pharmaceutical, energy, and technology sectors; and are interested in expanding cooperation in innovation, high technology, logistics, and precision engineering.
"I believe that the success of the Vietnam-EFTA Agreement is not measured by the number of tariff lines reduced, but by the projects implemented, technologies transferred, supply chains formed, and competitiveness enhanced," Minister Le Manh Hung affirmed.
Switzerland: A key partner in realizing opportunities.
As Vietnam's largest trading partner within EFTA, Switzerland plays a crucial role in promoting trade, investment, and technological cooperation between the two countries.
According to Vietnam Customs, in the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam-Switzerland trade reached US$806.2 million, an increase of 6.9%. As of September 30, 2026, Switzerland had 247 active projects in Vietnam, with a total registered capital of approximately US$2.5 billion, ranking 20th among 154 countries and territories investing in Vietnam.
In particular, Switzerland's strengths in technology, finance, and innovation can complement Vietnam's production capacity, dynamic markets, and integrated networks.
At the Switzerland-Vietnam Economic Forum Hanoi 2026, Swiss Federal President and Minister of Economy, Education and Research Guy Parmelin assessed that both sides still have many opportunities in advanced manufacturing, life sciences, healthcare, sustainable infrastructure, clean technology and digital transformation .
According to Mr. Guy Parmelin, VEFTA is not just a trade tool but also a strategic commitment, enhancing legal certainty and improving market access. “And perhaps most importantly, the Agreement sends a strong message of confidence in the future of economic relations between the two countries,” President Guy Parmelin affirmed.
You may also like
From a business perspective, Silvan Wildhaber, President of the Swiss Federation of Businesses (Economiesuisse), believes that the true success of an FTA must be reflected in daily business operations, whereby small and medium-sized enterprises can export more easily, and new value chains are formed.
Emphasizing the long-term investment orientation of Swiss businesses, Silvan Wildhaber expressed his hope that the two governments would soon establish a mechanism for regular dialogue between the public and private sectors, ensuring a transparent and consistent legal environment.
To realize this opportunity, Minister Le Manh Hung said that the Ministry of Industry and Trade will coordinate with other ministries and agencies to soon submit to the Government for approval and promulgation the implementation plan and related legal documents.
The Minister of Industry and Trade proposed that the two sides periodically exchange views on the progress of ratification, aiming to bring the Agreement into effect from the beginning of 2027; while also prioritizing the provision of information to small and medium-sized enterprises, and strengthening cooperation on rules of origin, quarantine, and technical barriers to trade.
For Vietnamese businesses, the long-term value of VEFTA is not only about expanding export markets, but also about opportunities to connect with technology, adopt advanced management practices, and improve their position in the supply chain. Switzerland is expected to be a key partner in this process.

articles.title: Policy credit helps women build economic independence - Vietnam Investment Review - VIR
articles.summary: Policy credit helps women build economic independence  Vietnam Investment Review - VIR
articles.full_text:
Pham Duc An, Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV), said that over the years, the SBV and the Vietnam Women's Union had signed and implemented numerous cooperation programmes to promote the nationwide implementation of the Party's and state's policies on monetary and banking matters.
“These initiatives have helped women gain easier access to credit and banking services to support production and business activities, care for their families, and improve their quality of life,” he said.
In this process, the Vietnam Bank for Social Policies (VBSP) plays an important role in providing preferential credit to eligible beneficiaries of government policy programmes. With the participation of the Women's Union at all levels, activities including entrusted lending, the management of savings and credit groups, policy communication, and the inspection and supervision of loan use are carried out at the grassroots level. This approach makes credit more accessible to local communities and also helps improve the management and effective use of funds.
According to VBSP, by the end of 2025, outstanding loans entrusted through the Women's Union at all levels of the VBSP had exceeded $6.14 billion, serving nearly 2.5 million borrowers. This demonstrates the scale and importance of the cooperative network in channelling policy credit to local communities, supporting production and improving incomes. In addition, Women's Union organisations at all levels have actively encouraged members to strengthen their financial literacy and legal awareness and choose formal borrowing channels. The effective operation of savings and credit groups, guidance on the proper use of loans, and monitoring of repayment have helped mitigate risks, improve credit quality, and prevent recourse to illegal lending.
| Photo: VBSP | 
A concrete example can be found in Van Han commune, Thai Nguyen province, where ethnic minority communities account for nearly half of the population. Local authorities, the VBSP, and the Women's Union work together to inform residents about and guide them in accessing preferential credit programmes through the Savings and Credit Group network.
"With policy credit, my family has shifted away from underperforming rice fields to cultivating tea," said Tran Thi Mai, a resident of Van Han commune, Thai Nguyen province. "In the past, my family struggled because we lacked a reliable livelihood and our income was unstable. After receiving a loan to improve the land and develop tea cultivation, our household income has nearly tripled."
Mai's experience illustrates the practical value of policy credit for women in rural and mountainous areas. Such funding enables people to invest in production while creating opportunities to increase incomes, stabilise livelihoods, and achieve greater economic independence.
According to Doan Le Thuy, director of the VBSP's Dong Hy Transaction Office in Thai Nguyen province, the bank is implementing more than 10 policy credit programmes with preferential interest rates, including loans to poor households at an annual rate of 6.24 per cent.
"Beyond enabling families to develop their livelihoods, these funds also help strengthen women's roles and standing in their communities," Thuy said. "When women have better opportunities to improve their household economies, they can enhance their living standards, gain confidence, and take a more active role in community activities and local initiatives."
More broadly, policy credit also enables women to expand production and business operations, develop startups, and create jobs for female workers. Under the Women's Entrepreneurship Support Scheme for 2026-2035, the target is for 80 per cent of Women's Union members to receive greater awareness of economic development and entrepreneurship through the Vietnam Women's Union by 2030.
According to a survey by the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry, women-owned businesses currently account for approximately 25 per cent of all enterprises. This highlights women's potential contribution to the economy while underscoring the need to expand access to finance and support the development of their production and business capabilities.
For policy credit to deliver lasting benefits, lending must go hand in hand with policy communication, improved financial literacy, and guidance on the proper use of funds. Through cooperation among the VBSP, the Vietnam Women's Union, and local authorities, policy credit continues to provide a foundation for women to develop sustainable livelihoods and increase their incomes, contributing to poverty reduction and social welfare.

articles.title: Moving closer to the 10% growth target. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Moving closer to the 10% growth target.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to Ms. Nguyen Thi Mai Hanh, Head of the National Accounts System Department (Statistics Bureau, Ministry of Finance ), the results achieved in the first nine months show that the economy is getting closer to the 10% growth target for the whole year, although there are still many challenges ahead. 
|  | 
| Ms. Nguyen Thi Mai Hanh, Head of the National Accounts System Department (Statistics Department, Ministry of Finance) | 
 After the first nine months of 2026, the economy has achieved remarkable growth results. Madam, what is the feasibility of achieving the 10% growth target for the whole year in the remaining months?  
 The target of 10% growth for the whole year of 2026 is an important direction for us to strive towards. In fact, the growth results in the first nine months show that the economy is undergoing positive changes and is getting closer to this target.
 Specifically, after updating information and data more comprehensively, the General Statistics Office recalculated and announced preliminary GDP growth rates of 8.15% for the first quarter, 8.81% for the second quarter, and 8.49% for the first six months of the year. These figures are all higher than the previously published estimates of 7.83%, 8.39%, and 8.18%, respectively. This result demonstrates the resilience of the economy more clearly with additional data available for calculation and evaluation.
 In the third quarter of 2026, GDP is estimated to grow by 9.95%, 1.82 percentage points higher than the 8.13% growth in the same period of 2025. For the first nine months of the year, GDP is estimated to grow by 9.01%, 1.21 percentage points higher than the same period last year. Notably, the growth rate in the third quarter has already approached double digits, reflecting the accelerating momentum of the economy.
 These are positive signs, laying the foundation for continued efforts in the fourth quarter. However, to achieve the 10% growth target for the whole year, GDP in the fourth quarter needs to increase by approximately 12.5%. This is a challenging task, requiring the continued strong promotion of production, investment, and consumption drivers; at the same time, ministries, sectors, and localities need to resolutely remove obstacles, accelerate the implementation of projects, and create favorable conditions for production and business activities.
 Entering the third quarter, the Government issued Resolution 168/NQ-CP, outlining many key solutions. How do you evaluate these solutions?  
 Following the Government's issuance of Resolution 168/NQ-CP, which updated the growth scenario and key solutions for the remaining quarters to achieve the 2026 growth target of 10% or more, ministries, sectors, and localities have become more actively involved and determined than ever before. The results achieved in the past three months have confirmed that the growth drivers continue to be promoted, notably industrial production, investment, trade, and tourism .
 These positive developments indicate that investment resources and market demand are being transformed into production and business activities, supporting economic growth. Encouragingly, public investment, the recovery of businesses, and domestic purchasing power still have room to contribute more strongly in Q4 2026 through accelerating project progress, removing obstacles, and boosting domestic demand.
 Overall, positive developments have been evident in industrial production, investment, trade, and services. Areas requiring further acceleration include the progress and spread of public investment, the resilience of businesses, and the purchasing power of the domestic market. The focus for Q4 2026 will be on removing bottlenecks in project implementation, accelerating the volume of work completed and payments settled, supporting businesses in expanding their export markets, and strengthening domestic demand to fully utilize growth resources. 
 According to her, what factors have actually translated into GDP growth?  
 The driving forces include accelerated industrial production, with the processing and manufacturing industry continuing to play a leading role in growth. The value added of the processing and manufacturing sector in the third quarter increased by 12.28% – the highest increase in many years. Specifically, the electronics, computer, and optical products sector increased by 18.67%; metal production by 17.4%; machinery and equipment by nearly 16%; and rubber and plastic product manufacturing by 14.67%… reflecting market demand and production activities that have truly created domestic added value.
 Investment resources have been put into practical use with the participation of all sectors. Total social investment in the third quarter of 2026 is estimated to increase by 16.7%; the overall increase for the first nine months is over 15%. | Real estate projects are increasingly following transportation infrastructure developments (Photo: Gia Anh) | 
 New supply is concentrated along the main roads.
 According to a report by Dat Xanh Services Research Institute, from 2025 onwards, the supply of new housing in Ho Chi Minh City and neighboring provinces such as Tay Ninh and Dong Nai will continue to be concentrated along major transportation routes, including ring roads, national highways, and metro lines.
 Data shows that new supply is concentrated along inter-regional transportation axes. Specifically, the area around Ring Road 2 has nearly 7,000 housing units under development; Ring Road 3 has 11,066 units, and Ring Road 4 has approximately 15,469 units. Along National Highway 13, which previously connected Ho Chi Minh City with Binh Duong, there are over 11,090 real estate projects under development. Tens of thousands of other apartments are also being developed around National Highway 1K, the My Phuoc - Tan Van Expressway, and the former Metro Line 2 in Binh Duong.
 The data also shows a significant increase in real estate supply along transportation routes after construction projects were implemented. According to Batdongsan.com.vn, in the period 2020-2025, Ho Chi Minh City and its suburbs around Ring Roads 2, 3, and 4 had 324 apartment projects. To date, this number has increased to approximately 1,050 projects, mostly located within a radius of 20-40 km from the city center, along Ring Roads 3 and 4. 
 In the medium and long term, infrastructure-dependent real estate is projected to continue as public investment is boosted and multi-centered urban models gradually take shape. However, transportation infrastructure only truly plays its role when it is seamlessly connected to housing, employment, and essential amenities.  Along the Metro Line 2 route, from the intersection of National Highway 13 and National Highway 1K in Binh Duong (formerly), only 5 projects were developed during the 2020-2024 period. From 2025 to the present, approximately 20 new projects have emerged, including Diamond Sky, Happi One Mori, Ava Center, Habitat, A&T Saigon Riverside, Thuan An 1 & 2, One Era, Bcons New Sky, Emerald Garden View, Ho Guom Xanh, etc.
 Similarly, along the Ben Luc - Long Thanh expressway, the number of real estate projects was limited before construction. After the expressway was put into operation, many new projects began to be announced. In 2026, Five Star Group announced the development of the Five Eco City project, covering 660 hectares and comprising townhouses, villas, and apartments.
 Mr. Phung Quang Hai, General Director of Five Star Group, said that after the Ben Luc - Long Thanh expressway passes through the area, the investor has started developing the project, with the apartment units expected to be launched in the fourth quarter of 2026.
 Along National Highway 1K and the My Phuoc - Tan Van Expressway, transportation routes connecting Ho Chi Minh City with the former Binh Duong and Dong Nai areas, a series of apartment projects by investors such as Bcons, Phu Dong Group, Hung Thinh, TBS Group, Gamuda Land, Le Phong, and An Gia have been implemented from 2024 to the present, with a total scale of tens of thousands of units.
 Notably, the 2027 plans of companies such as Van Xuan Group, Phu Dong Group, and Bcons show that many new projects will continue to be concentrated along these transportation routes, with a total expected supply of over 7,000 units, mainly apartment units.
 Not only has supply increased, but real estate prices around transportation routes have also risen. Observations show that in the area along National Highway 13, housing prices have increased from 35-40 million VND/m2 in 2025 to 55-70 million VND/m2. Prices on other roads have also increased by approximately 20-30%.
 Ms. Cao Thi Thanh Huong, Deputy Director of the Real Estate Market Research and Consulting Department (Savills Ho Chi Minh City), believes that when house prices in the central area remain high, buyers must carefully consider location, connectivity, and affordability. This is also when infrastructure becomes a crucial factor, contributing to expanding the development space of the housing market.
 Distance to the city center still matters, but it's no longer the sole criterion. Areas with better transport links, shorter commute times, and more accessible housing prices may become attractive alternatives for homebuyers.
 This trend is reflected in the supply and transaction structure in Ho Chi Minh City. In the low-rise housing segment, almost all new supply comes from suburban areas, while two large-scale urban areas in the North and South account for over 90% of total market transactions.
 In the long term, the supply from major cities and suburban areas with connected infrastructure can expand options for real homebuyers, at more affordable prices. According to Ms. Huong, location advantages are increasingly valued not only in terms of distance to the city center, but also in terms of connectivity, price, and quality of life.
 Transportation infrastructure needs to go hand in hand with urban amenities.
 Dr. Vu Xuan Dung, Director of Design Division 2 (Bcons Group), believes that in the period 2025-2030, the Southern region will witness the implementation of a series of large-scale technical infrastructure projects, from Ring Road 3 and Ring Road 4 to metro lines and inter-regional transportation axes. These are important conditions for expanding development space.
 However, transportation only solves the connectivity problem. Whether people choose to live and settle down long-term depends largely on the social infrastructure.
 “An area with convenient roads but lacking schools, medical facilities, shopping centers, and essential services cannot yet constitute a complete living environment. Therefore, I believe that technical and social infrastructure must be planned and invested in synchronously from the outset, rather than focusing on transportation first and then considering amenities for the people,” Mr. Dung said.
 According to Mr. Dung, urban development should stem from the actual needs of each resident group. Young families need affordable housing with clear legal documentation; professionals working in industrial zones need convenient living and commuting; and students and lecturers need living environments close to universities and public transportation. Each group has its own needs, therefore urban products need to be developed accordingly.
 Mr. Dung believes that private enterprises can contribute additional resources alongside the State to solve urban problems, especially in developing affordable housing and essential amenities. The important thing is to put the needs of the people at the center, so that cities not only expand in scale but also truly become livable places.
 For his part, Mr. Le Nguyen Bao Trong, Director of the Economic and Technical Department (Becamex Group), noted that Ho Chi Minh City is facing four structural bottlenecks that need to be addressed: network infrastructure, urban space, the integration of human resources with science, technology and innovation, and mechanisms for connecting resources. These issues are closely related, requiring Ho Chi Minh City to adopt a synchronized approach in its development process.
 "The challenge now is not just about solving individual problems or implementing more projects, but about changing the development approach, from developing each region to developing the ecosystem, from removing individual bottlenecks to addressing infrastructure, mechanisms, and resources in a coordinated manner," Mr. Trong emphasized.
 Mr. Nguyen Quoc Anh, Deputy General Director of Batdongsan.com.vn, affirmed that the trend of real estate development based on infrastructure is contributing to the restructuring of urban space towards a multi-centered approach, reducing pressure on the core area. However, effectiveness is only achieved when housing development is accompanied by synchronized planning of social infrastructure, employment, and services. Without these elements, the risk of forming lifeless urban areas remains.
 In the medium and long term, infrastructure-dependent real estate is projected to continue as public investment is boosted and multi-centered urban models gradually take shape. However, transportation infrastructure only truly plays its role when it is seamlessly connected to housing, employment, and essential amenities.
 This means that the market's advantage no longer lies solely in projects being near major roads or anticipating transportation infrastructure, but also in the potential to create urban areas with complete living conditions. This will also be a decisive factor in the attractiveness and sustainability of real estate in the South in the coming period.

BEIJING, Oct. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — When the 2026 North Bund Forum was held in Shanghai recently, around 4,000 participants gathered at the North Bund to build deeper consensus on global shipping win-win cooperation.
As a flagship event for the shipping sector, the forum featured over 60 sessions. Together with related events, more than 15,000 people including foreign peers from over 50 countries and regions gathered in the eastern China metropolis.
Arsenio Dominguez, Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), called for resilience and cooperation in the global shipping industry against the backdrop of technological transformation, energy transition and challenges stemming from complex geopolitical situations.

Academy of Sciences Malaysia fellow Jayum Jawan said the Muslim Malay-Melanau community had little reason to switch to PAS.

Jayum was commenting on PAS’s intention to contest four seats in the upcoming state election, including Samariang, Sebuyau and Beting Maro. It won its first state seat in Sabah last November.
Sarawak PAS chief Arifiriazul Paijo said the state leadership had submitted a proposal for the central leadership’s decision.

articles.summary: The bank is supplementing its lending resources with international capital.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Expanding funding sources from international institutions.
 By the end of September 2026, the total mobilized capital of banks nationwide reached VND 19.5 million billion, an increase of 10.7% compared to the end of 2025, while total credit to the economy reached over VND 20.7 million billion, an increase of 11.7%. The demand for capital to serve economic development is very large, while the dependence on the banking system continues to put pressure on resource mobilization and balancing.
 Dr. Can Van Luc, Chief Economist and Director of the BIDV Training and Research Institute, estimates that during the period 2026–2030, total social investment capital needs to increase by an average of approximately 13–15% per year, equivalent to a capital requirement of about 280–300 billion USD per year. In this context, the challenge is not only to mobilize sufficient capital but also to diversify capital channels, reduce dependence on the banking system, and improve the efficiency of resource allocation.
 For banks, expanding access to international capital markets is a way to supplement resources to meet the financing needs of businesses and the economy. Recently, HDBank raised a syndicated international loan worth US$721 million, coordinated and arranged by Standard Chartered and the Asian Development Bank (ADB). The loan aims to support small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and expand sustainable financial activities. 
|  | 
| The increasing demand for capital in the economy is prompting banks to expand their fundraising efforts in international markets. | 
 The loan amount increased by approximately 60% compared to the initial plan of $450 million. Previously, HDBank also raised $270 million in green capital and $380 million in sustainable finance capital from international institutions, including IFC, ADB, and JICA.
 At VPBank , at the end of June 2026, the bank signed a sustainable syndicated loan agreement worth US$1.44 billion with 15 international financial institutions. In the first half of the year, MB completed raising US$550 million in foreign loans through syndicated and bilateral loans, with the participation of Standard Chartered, Wells Fargo, LBBW, and OCBC.
VIB also finalized a 3-year syndicated loan worth US$285 million from nine international financial institutions. This is part of the bank's plan to raise US$1 billion in medium and long-term capital from international markets in 2026.
 On October 12, 2026,SHB also announced the signing of a loan agreement coordinated by Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), with an initial size of US$340 million, which may be increased depending on the terms of the agreement, with a term of three years from the date of the first disbursement, to provide credit and finance eligible projects. This transaction follows two syndicated loans under ESG criteria totaling US$600 million raised in 2025 with the participation of 26 international financial institutions.
 According to SHB, developing international capital raising channels aims to strengthen the structure of medium and long-term capital sources, enhance flexibility in resource management, and strengthen the ability to meet business development needs. Options are considered based on capital utilization needs, market conditions, raising costs, and operational safety requirements, while also complying with legal regulations.
 The fundraising activities of international financial institutions also demonstrate the demand for capital from this market. According to Standard Chartered's announcement at the end of September 2026, since the beginning of the year, the bank has supported Vietnamese businesses and financial institutions in raising approximately US$3.3 billion in the international market. The total value is expected to reach nearly US$7 billion by the end of the year.
 The transactions and fundraising plans show that the bank is expanding its resources beyond domestic deposits. These include several loans aimed at supporting small and medium-sized enterprises, developing green and sustainable finance, and supplementing term capital for business operations.
 Balancing maturity, costs, and exchange rate risks.
 The value of international capital lies not only in the scale of mobilization but also in its ability to supplement medium and long-term capital, diversify capital providers, and improve the bank's resource structure. However, access to capital needs to be considered along with the costs and future debt repayment obligations.
 According to Mr. Nguyen Quang Thuan, Chairman of FiinGroup and FiinRatings, although international interest rates remain high and even risk increasing, international capital, mostly medium and long-term, still plays a role in meeting long-term capital needs and improving the foreign exchange position of credit institutions.
 Banks' pursuit of international funding is not simply driven by the goal of raising capital at low cost. Given the rapidly increasing demand for long-term capital in the economy, while the bank's capital structure remains heavily skewed towards short-term funding, the maturity of financing and the ability to diversify funding sources are crucial factors to consider.
 With loans having long maturities, banks have additional resources to balance their medium- and long-term financing needs. However, raising capital in foreign currency does not always mean lower capital costs. If a bank raises capital in foreign currency but uses it to finance in Vietnamese Dong, it must also factor in the cost of hedging against exchange rate risks and balancing cash flow.
 A representative from Standard Chartered also noted that the conditions for raising international capital depend on the performance of US Treasury bond yields, inflation expectations, geopolitical situations, and investors' risk appetite. Therefore, access to large sources of capital must be considered alongside the cost of raising funds and risk management requirements.
 From the perspective of domestic capital balance, SSI Research assesses that the core issue of the current economy lies more in capital sources than in aggregate demand. According to SSI Research, the large gap between credit growth and deposit mobilization keeps the cost of capital high, while asset quality may be affected if the absorption capacity of the real estate market weakens.
 Under these circumstances, foreign capital can contribute to reducing dependence on domestic deposits and expanding the maturity structure. However, the effectiveness of mobilization is only fully realized when the capital is used appropriately, generating cash flow to meet debt repayment obligations and ensuring profitability after accounting for all related costs.
 The need for capital balance becomes even more important as Vietnam implements a roadmap to improve banking safety standards towards the Basel III approach. Expanding credit, diversifying funding sources, and ensuring resilience to risks need to be considered simultaneously.
 According to experts, syndicated loans, bilateral loans, and international bond issuance plans are opening up more fundraising options for banks. For these resources to be effective, each option needs to be linked to capital needs, financing terms, risk mitigation costs, and repayment capacity. This also forms the basis for international capital to support banks in maintaining their ability to supply capital to the economy while ensuring operational safety.

articles.title: Retail investors face changing Vietnam stock market landscape: expert - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Retail investors face changing Vietnam stock market landscape: expert  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Retail investors today are different from those of the past as they are more cautious, selective and demanding when it comes to corporate transparency and business quality, writes Nguyen The Minh, head of investment banking at An Binh Securities JSC (ABS).
A year of milestones and market turbulence
I have followed Vietnam’s stock market for more than 17 years, through multiple cycles of euphoria and panic. Yet few years have seen expectations and real developments intertwine as complexly as 2026.
Structurally, 2026 is a historic year for the market. FTSE Russell has confirmed Vietnam’s reclassification to Secondary Emerging Market status, effective September 21. Vietnamese stocks will be included in FTSE indices in four tranches, with respective allocation weights of 10%, 20%, 35% and 35%, through September 2027.
The milestone reflects years of reforms, including the removal of pre-funding requirements, the introduction of a global brokerage model, a new trading system and a legal framework increasingly aligned with international standards.
The investor base has also expanded significantly. By the end of August 2026, the market had about 13.83 million domestic investor accounts, equivalent to nearly 14% of the population. More than 2 million new accounts were opened in the first eight months of the year, almost all by individual investors.
Yet price movements have made 2026 a challenging year. The VN-Index, which represents the Ho Chi Minh Stock Exchange (HoSE), started the year at around 1,830-1,880 points before falling nearly 11% in March. In April, the index rebounded by more than 10% after the market reclassification was confirmed, and briefly hit a record high above 1,930 points in May. The market subsequently retreated to the 1,715-1,760 range in July and August.
Notably, on September 21, the official reclassification date, the VN-Index fell nearly 16 points, slipping below the 1,800-point mark. The index lost around 3.5% over the month as a whole. Trading liquidity on the HoSE fell to around VND10 trillion ($386.95 million) in matched orders on some sessions. In October, the market recorded a seven-session losing streak amid subdued liquidity and net selling by foreign investors.
The year’s most striking paradox is that the index has risen, yet most investors do not feel wealthier. Gains have been concentrated in a small group of large-cap stocks, particularly those in the Vingroup ecosystem.
Excluding these stocks, the VN-Index’s gain since the start of the year would be roughly half as large. At one point, the index traded at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of around 13 times, while more than 70% of other stocks had P/E ratios below 10 times.
This backdrop has made retail investor sentiment more complex than ever and raised the bar for those responsible for operating the market.
Retail investors optimistic about the long term, skeptical about the short term
Based on what I have observed through our client network and meetings with investors, the current mindset of retail investors can be summed up in one phrase: conditional optimism.
They are not pessimistic. The steady increase in new accounts, averaging around 250,000 a month even during periods of sharp market declines, is evidence of this. It shows that confidence in equities as a vehicle for wealth accumulation has spread much more widely than in the past. People no longer view stocks as a gamble, but as an investment option alongside savings, gold and real estate.
However, they are no longer as euphoric as they were in 2020-2021. Back then, most new investors entered the market during a powerful uptrend, when almost every stock was rising and money invested tended to generate returns. In 2026, the market is far more polarized. Investors holding the leading stocks have generally earned strong returns, while those with diversified exposure to mid- and small-cap stocks are likely still sitting on losses, even as the index trades near record highs.
I divide retail investors today into four main psychological groups.
Long-term investors. These are typically investors who have lived through at least one market crisis, such as those in 2018 or 2022. They use market corrections to accumulate leading stocks with strong fundamental growth and the ability to attract capital flows. They rely less on leverage and are less concerned about short-term fluctuations. This group is growing, which is an encouraging sign.
Short-term traders. This group still accounts for a large share of trading liquidity. Its members react quickly to news, capital flows and technical signals. In a market characterized by sharp divergence and a lack of broad-based rallies, they face the greatest pressure, as short-lived gains often fail to offset trading costs and risks.
Investors waiting on the sidelines. These investors have accounts and available capital but are temporarily staying out of the market. They are waiting for clearer signals, such as improved liquidity, sustained net buying by foreign investors or a broader rally across sectors. In my view, this group represents the market’s largest pool of potential capital.
Investors who have withdrawn. Some investors, particularly those who used high margin leverage or suffered heavy losses, have shifted their money into savings, gold or real estate. They still have stock trading accounts but are largely inactive. 
What all four groups have in common is greater caution and selectivity. Investors are increasingly asking about corporate quality, valuations and capital flows rather than simply asking, “Which stocks are going up?” This is a sign of a market gradually maturing, although the process will inevitably involve setbacks.
Another notable phenomenon is the feeling that the market is rising but investors are not happy. When the VN-Index remains near elevated levels but most portfolios fail to gain proportionately, investors can become frustrated and skeptical. Many are beginning to feel that the index no longer reflects their own investment experience. If this persists, the biggest risk may not be falling prices, but the gradual erosion of investor confidence.
Even so, greater caution does not mean retail capital has turned its back on the market. Several solid underlying factors continue to underpin confidence and encourage some investors to deploy capital.
In my view, four factors are supporting retail investor confidence.
First, the market reclassification represents a long-term structural shift. Reclassification is not a one-day event; it opens the door to capital from global index-tracking and actively managed funds. With the allocation schedule extending through September 2027, passive inflows will be phased in over multiple periods.
More importantly, FTSE reclassification paves the way for the next objective: an upgrade by Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI), whose tracked assets are substantially larger. Long-term investors understand that the market may be entering the early stages of a revaluation cycle.
Second, valuations are becoming attractive. Following market corrections, the VN-Index’s P/E ratio has at times fallen about 20% below its long-term average. Many leading companies, particularly those outside the stocks driving the index higher, are trading at single-digit P/E multiples despite continued earnings growth.
For investors with a two- to three-year investment horizon, these valuations offer an opportunity to accumulate stocks with a reasonable margin of safety.
Third, macroeconomic fundamentals and corporate earnings remain solid. Vietnam continues to post strong economic growth relative to the region, while public investment is accelerating, credit is recovering and domestic consumption is improving.
Q2/2026 earnings of listed companies rose by more than 25% year-on-year. When businesses remain profitable, investors have reason to believe that share prices will eventually reflect their underlying value.
Fourth, market infrastructure and the investment experience are improving. Opening an account online takes just minutes, trading fees are becoming increasingly competitive, and investment options have expanded to include open-ended funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and fund certificates. Several open-ended funds have recorded one-year returns of more than 30%, suggesting that indirect investment channels are delivering tangible results for investors who lack the time to monitor the market.
Investors who are confident enough to commit capital at this stage tend to share one characteristic: they focus on businesses rather than stock price screens. They accept short-term volatility in pursuit of long-term opportunities and invest in stages rather than committing all their capital at once.
However, the investor sentiment picture is not entirely positive.
Alongside these positive factors, there are plenty of reasons for retail investors to remain hesitant. In my view, six main factors are holding them back.
The first is the “buy the rumor, sell the news” effect. Expectations of Vietnam’s market reclassification had been priced in months before the event. When the status upgrade officially took effect, speculative investors took profits, sending the market lower on the day itself. Many retail investors who had bought in anticipation of the event were left on the back foot. The experience has made them more cautious about investment themes receiving widespread media attention.
Second, foreign capital inflows have fallen short of expectations. Many investors assumed that the reclassification would trigger an immediate surge in net foreign buying. In reality, the initial allocation tranche accounts for just 10%, while actively managed funds have continued to record net selling at various points amid exchange-rate pressures, global interest rates and regional portfolio rebalancing. The gap between expectations and reality has diminished the appeal of the reclassification story as a short-term catalyst.
